Days dawn on us that make amends for many Sometimes, When heaven and earth seem sweeter even than any Man's rhymes. Light had not all been quenched in France, or quelled In Greece, Had Homer sung not, or had Hugo held
, is peace. ilad Sappho's self not left her word thus long For token, The sea round Lesbos yet in waves of song Had spoken.

And yet these days of subtler air and finer Delight, Wher lovelier looks the darkness, and diviner The light. The gift they give of all these golden hours, Whose urn Pours forth reverberate rays or shadowing showers In turn. Clouds,beams, and winds. that make the live day's track •Seem living— What were they did no spirit give them back. Thanksgiving?

Dead air, dead fire, dead shapes and shadows, telling Time nought; Man gives them sense and soul by song, and dwelling In thought. In human thought their being endures, their power Abides: Else were their life a thing that each light hour
Derides.

The years live, work, sigh, smile, and die, with all They cherish; The soul endures, though dreams that fed it fall And perish. 3 in human thought have all things habitation; Our days L augh, lower, and lighten past, and find no station That stays. But thought and faith are mightier things than time
Can wrong, Made splendid once with speech, or made sublime
By song. Remembrance, though the tide of change that rolls —7..
Wax hoary, Gives earth and heaven, for song's sake and the soul's, Their glory. ALGERNON' CHARLES SWINEURNE.
—English Illustrated.

It is easier to make peace in Europe than to adjust a 'quarrel between htvo women.—Lemis XIV.: It is not a badluality in a woman to be learned, but it is a very bad one for her to have the affectation of learning.—La Fontaine. There is not one quality that is truly amiable in a man which is not equally so in woman and there is not one vice or folly which ought not to be equally detestable in both. Education is not that which smothers a *omen with accomplishments, but that which tends to constitute a firm and regular character—to form a friend, a com- panion and a wife.—Hannah More. A modern philosopher thinks it a mistake to suppose women have stronger attachments than men. A man is n•often attached to an old hat; but, he asks "Who ever heard of a woman being attached to an old bonnet ?" It is a mistake to suppose that a woman with no heart will be an easy creditor in the exchange of affection. -There is not on earth a more merciless exacter of love from others than a thoroughly selfish woman; and the more unlovely she grows the more jealously she exacts love.—Mrs. Stowe. A man will carry twenty sovereigns in his waistcoat pocket, but a woman needs a morocco portemonnaie as large as one's fist, and too heavy to be carried in the pocket, to escort five shillings, a couple of postage stamps, a recipe for making curry-powder, and two pat- terns of dress goods. ' --- Here is what General Gordon, in his "Reflections in Palestine," says of the tongue and the ladies :—" The tongue is glib, serpent-like, and it is odd that women have it in such perfection, which none have ever doubted. It is their defence. The woman ate first, and the tongue is her particular forte. Yet when women speak good, how well they speak it out! They are in this point the salt of the earth." Addressing a young lady, Sydney Smith says, "Do you over reflect how-you pass your life? If you live te seventy-two, which I hope you may, your life is passed in the following manner:—An hour a day is three years. This makes twenty-seven years sleeping, nine years. dressing, nine years at table, six years playing with chil- dren, nine years walking, drawing, and visiting; six years shopping, and three years quarrelling." A peasant threw himself at the feet of Charles XII. ef Sweden, with a complaint against one of his grenadiers, that had robbed him and his family of their dinner "Is it true," said Charles sternly to the grenadier, "that you have robbed this man?" The soldier replied, "Sir, I have not done so much harm to this man as your Majesty has done to his master; for you have taken from Augustus a kingdom, but I have only taken from this peasant a dinner." Charles made the peasant amends, and he pardoned the grenadier for his bold re- monstrance, saying, "My friend, you will do well to recollect that if I took Poland from Augustus I !did net take it myself." We have a curious example of the difference between the false and the true in Dr. Chalmers. While in his dubious state the doctor was a great actor; subsequently the artist modified his action very perceptibly. It is little known that before the change in his religious senti- ments, he indulged in a considerable amount of gesticu- lation in the pulpit. 9ne day soon after his induction into Kilmany parish, he preached a sermon with even more than usual animation. Alter service a tenant in the parish, a sturdy trooper in the regiment of Fifeshire yeomanry cavalry, commanded by Colonel Anstruther -Thomson, the proprietor of Kilmany, remarked, "Eli, vrasna the minister grawnd the' day? It was guid as a • dreeling i' the sword exerceese." DANCING AS ENERCISE.—In a note the St. James's •Vazette has the following :—ln his lecture on "Mind and .Music" delivered a few days ago at the Birmingham 'Teachers' Association, Dr. Crichton Browne delivered a eulogium on dancing which would have rejoiced the heart of the dancing master in the "Bourgeois Geatil- homme." After some very interesting remarks on tbe educational value of different kinds of muscle work, he added that dancing, if taught at the proper time—that is, very early in life—" may discipline large groups of centres into harmonious action, enlarge the dominion of the Will, abolish unseemly muscular tricks and antics, develop the sense of equilibrium, and impart grace and self-confidence." Dr. Browne then gave a vivid picture .of the awkwardness displayed at a Scotch funeral by some 200 of the elite of a Scotch University city, few of whom could be suspected of having learned to dance." " Most curious was it to notice the facial contortions practised to express a sense of love and syrdpathy. Gross exaggeration was the commonest fault; and somethileS attempts to avoid this ended in an aspect of callous in- difference or positive enjoyment." Dr. Crichton Browne came to the conclusion that evenithe most distinguished of his countrymen were sadly deficient in muscle cul- ture, and that they should have been taught dancing in. theiryouth—" not Scotch reels (though these are very well in their way), but graceful and grace-giving dances." THE VILLAGE AGRICULTURE OF OUR ANCESTORS.—Our ancestors indeed would have been surprised had they been told that their descendants would value 'commons mainly as peculiarly charming recreation grounds. The •copimon was as essential to their agricultural system as the ploughed fields or the meadows. Tillage was not then an affair of individual judgment or fancy. Each parish or viii was in fact one farm, cultivated by the inhabitants in common according to strict rules. The arable lands lay in three large fie'ds, or in two or three sets of such fields. One field of each triplet was sown with an autumn crop, one with a spring crop, and the third lay fallow. When the crops were off, the cattle of the village roamed over the stubble; and when the meadows were not shut up for hay, they afforded rich pasture. But in the summer, when corn and grass were growing, the common was the only place where any feed was to be had, for there were no separate inclosures of any size. The oxen which drew the great village ploughs, working eight, twelve, or even sixteen in a team, the 'dairy cows:the young stock, and the sheep must all to a considerable extent have relied upon the common for support during the early summer months. Nor was it for its feed alone that the common was invaluable. The fencing of the fields to prevent the intrusion of cattle when the crops were growing, the ploughs and carts of the village, and even its houses required a constant supply of wood, and for this recourse was had mainly to the common. In old Court Rolls we find constant direc- tions to the tenants to make up the hedges of the com- mon fields, each owner being responsible for the portion bordering upon the strips which he tilled,; and regula— tions as to the mode of cutting the wood on the common are equally frequent. The furze and smaller scrub, again, were valuable for fuel, and the brake and heath made good litter and served afterwards for manure. Even the wild fruits of the common were not despised. In the time of Henry VIII. persons were fined by the Manor Court for gathering crab-apples on Wimbledon , Common, and it is piteously complained that by reason of this lawless act "the tenants of the land cannot have their apples growing upon the common aforesaid accord- ing to their rate as from ancient time they were accus- tomed." Fruit can hardly have been very plentiful when crab-apples were solemnly apportioned to the tenants ~of a manor within seven miles of the City in accordance with the extent of their holdings. lamezenea.—The main cause of nervousness is indigestion, and that le caused by weakness of the stomach. A School Board Examiner lately asked the following questions of a little girl:—"What is the plural of man 7" "Men." Very well; and what is the plural of child?" "Twins," immediately replied the little girl. Smith:l notice that milkmen as a rule wear very heavy shoes. Brown: Yes; they do it on purposep guess. Smith: Why? Brown: Because, you know, it would be rather suggestive if you could say they used pumps. , Agitations are the opportunities and means God offers us to refine the taste, mould the character, lift the pur- pose, and educate the moral. senses of the masses, on whose intelligence and self-respect rests the state.— Wendell Phillips. "Pa," asked the small boy, "Why do they call the first piece the organ plays in church the 'voluntary?" "Because, my son," replied the old gentleman, the organist runs his hands over the keys, and the organ goes wherever it pleases." Sciitchman : "What'll y' haer —Frenchman "I vill take a drop of contradiction."--Scotchman : "What's that ?"—Frenchman: "Veil, you put in de whisky to make it strong, de water to make it weak, de lemon to make it sour, and de sugar to make it sweet. Den you say 'Here's to you!' and you take it yourself." The other day, after a wheezy old hand organ had been played for ten minutes in front of a suburban residence, the owner descended the steps and asked—" Do you ex- pect to be paid for standing here and grinding out such a noise?" "Well, sir, some pay me for grinding out the noise, and some pay me for stopping it and moving on. You can take your choice." Here is the last of a shoemaker, beyond which let no cobbler go. A lady complaining that the soles of her ' shoes were too thick, the artful manufacturer said to her, "Is that your only objection to them, madam ?" "It is," the lady replied. "Well, then, madam, if you'll take them, r think I can assure you that you will And that objection gradually wear away." The truth may cost many a pang to utter, strict integ- rity may have to give up many a coveted gain, the cour- age of:principle may forfeit the goodwill so highly prized or the position so eminently desirable; but upon the scale of years they will lead their adherents to a condition of honour and happiness compared with which all that had been sacrificed seems utterly trivial. There is no way of repressing feeling so effectual as to deny its expression. The very effort so to calm the tones of our voice as to express less anger than one feels will of itself allay the anger and bring about a milder mood. The brave struggle to endure necessary suffering without inflicting cries and lamentations upon friends will en- hance one's power of endurance. He who resolutely changes a whining and fretful tone for a cheerful one will soon find much less to fret about. A stupid-looking recruit halted before a blacksmith's forge, the proprietor of which was forging a shoe, and • eyed the performance with much interest. The brawny smith, dissatisfied with the man's curiosity, held the red- hot iron suddenly: under his nose, hoping to make him beats hasty retreat. "If you give me half-a-crown I'll lick it," said the soldier. The smith took from his pocket half-a-crown, and held it out. The cunning son of Mars took the coin, licked it, and walked away, whistling, "The girl I left behind me." An American general had some shirts made at a fashionablelmsier's, and the cutter, a tew weeks later, met the general walking with a friend. The general remembered the man's face, but that was all; and the cutter greeted him with, "Good morning, general. How are you to-day ?" The general stopped, shook hands, and the cutter, perceiving that the general's mind needed refreshing, said quietly, "Made your shirts." "Oh, beg pardon !" said the general quickly; and, turn- ing to the gentleman with whom he was walking, he said, "Colonel, allow me to introduce you to my friend, Major Schurz !" When once the desire of making money outside and in excess of the need of spending it takes possession of a man, and becomes his ideal of happiness, he has aban- doned all chance of the reality. He will never have enough—never! The desire of wealth is like that of fame, of place. Get to the top of this near peak, which seems to you to be the ultimate of your ambition, and which, when won, will land you on the pinnacle of your hope, and you will find that others, still higher and far- ther, will reveal themselves before you as points to be gained. If you, do not gain them, then has all your pre- vious success been in vain, and you are relatively no better off than when you began. AN ANGEL IN IT.—The great Florentine sculptor one day went into the civic stoneyard, and saw the blocks of marble lying about, and said, pointing to one, "What is the reason that beautiful stone is cast aside?" and he was told that it had already been in the studio of one great sculptor, who had returned it'as unfit for use. "Let me have it," he replied; "there is an angel in it, and if you will give it to me I will return it to you to decorate your city." That block of marble, in the hand of the great artist, became one of the most splendid pieces of sculpture that the world has ever seen. And so it is with us. The stone whieh men refuse as worth- less becomes, under the mighty hand of God, a living stone, ready for His Temple, lasting for evermore. "Strategy," says a writer in a contemporary, "is a thing to be admired when it is employed for the circum- vention of rogues. While the French were in Mexico, stage robberies on the Monterey-road became very fre- quent. The French commander resolved to put a stop to them, and this is how he did it :—He dressed up half a dozen Zouaves in ladies' attire, and sent them on in the next stage, their faces hidden by veils, their carbines hidden by their petticoats. The stage was stopped, the ladies, without waiting to be invited, left the vehicle and fell into line with the rest of the passengers. Suddenly a series of reports,came from that line, and some dozen robbers lay dead; the rest discreetly disappeared. Fora long while afterwards it was only requisite to display a shawl and bonnet conspicuously, to secure a free passage' for a stage on that road." THE FLIGHT OF TIME.—The flight of time is very per- ceptible in advanced life. Every year seems swifter than its precursor. Life seems impelled onward by an irre- sistible power. The departing year seems to draw its successor after it with an augmented force. As in spring every day becomes longer and in autumn eery day becomes shorter, so in the autumn of life every day, Seems to be curtailed. We are made sensible of the flight of time by the circumstances that surround us. One generation has passed away since we commenced life; another generation is springing up around ,US. There is a chronology written in our frames. Grey hairs, faltering steps, and failing faculties are the year book of nature. With many of us our years have been spent, and are not in expectation. We look back on ,life, not forward. The tale is hearty told; the last inci- cidents are crowding together, the last words are struggling for utterance, the last moments are being whirled away. While we are absorbed in the interest of the story, the speaker stops and the tale is ended.—Hay- croft. THE ENRAGED Airrisr.—The artist Turner, happening one day to pass a print•shop, noticed in the window a copy of one of the engravings from his famous " Liber Studiorum." The print was in a very dirty, ragged state, and Turner naturally felt aggrieved at seeing the work of his hands in this dilapidated condition. Enter- ing the shop, he proceeded at once to blame the master in no measured terms for having neglected so valuable a print, and for having allowed it to become so disfigured. The man protested that it was no fault of his, as he did but offer the engraving for sale in the same state in which he had bought it from some other dealer. This did not satisfy Turner, however; add he and the man continued arguing in this fashion for some time, each making the other more angry by contradiction. At last, the print-seller lost all patience. "Perhaps, sir," he said, "when you have quite finished what you have to say, you will kindly tell me what you have to do with this engraving, and what business it is of yours whether the print is clean or dirty ?" "This is what I have to do with it," answered the enraged artist. "It was I who drew the original of that print. My name is Turner, and I drew every line of that engraving with my own hand. Now do you wonder that I am angry at seeing my work in so disgraceful a state ?" "Indeed, sir," replied the print-seller, "so you are the great artist himself. All my life long it has been my wish that I might some day have the good fqrtune to see Mr. Turner. And, now that I have seen hind, I sincerely hope that I may never see him any more." POPE'S HHAD.—By some of Pope's biographers it is asserted that the head of the poet was abstracted from his coffin during some repairs of the church. On this subject Mr. Hewitt, in his Homes and Haunts of the British Poets," writes as follows:—" By one of those ants which neither science nor curiosity can excuse, the skull of Pope is now in the private collection of a phreno- logist. The manner in which it was obtained is said to have been this :—On some occasion of alteration in the church, or burial of some one in the same spot, the coffin of Pope was disinterred, and opened, to see the state of the remains. By a bribe to the sexton of the time, pos- session was obtained for the night, and another skull returned instead of it. I have heard that fifty pounds were paid to manage and carry through this transaction. Be that as it may, the undoubted skull of Pope now figures in the phrenological collection of Mr. Holm, of Highgate, and was frequently exhibited by him in his lectures, as demonstrating, by its not large but well- balanced proportions, its affinity to the intellectual char- acter of the poet." "Such statements," observes Mr. Cobbett, "are hard to bp disproved, more especially when Motives of interest support them., It is fair, how- ever, to the Rev. Charles Proby (the vicar during whose' time the alleged theft was committed), and to the then officials of the church, to give, as he communicated it to Mr. Powell, his churchwarden, his unqualified denial of each and every part of the story. Mr. Proby had seen Mr. Howitt's paragraph, and desired, as he was too old to enter into a paper war, thit the real facts which gave rise to the report should be published, if a new history of Twickenham were ever written. Mr. Froby's state- ment is as follows Upon opening a vault some years ago in the middle aisle of the church, adjoining Pope's, the latter fell in, the coffin was broken, and disclosed the pkeleton, which was very short, with (1. large skull. I was immediately informed of it, when I directed'my curate, Mr. Fletcher, to remain in the church, and not to leave until the whole was restored and built up. A cast • of the skull was taken, with my permission, by the mason employed, who well knew how to accomplish it. lam • quite sure that Mr. Fletcher rigidly carried out my in- structions. No such abstraction could have been made." ---Cassell'e "Greater London," for October. EAT'S Tic Pius, a specific in Neuralgia, leace,ehe, dui„ IS lid. lineage Id. Bold by Chfmlats Ray, Brother. THE NEW PARLLAMENT.—An analysis of the Redistribu- tion of Seats Act of last session shows that the 670 repre- sentatives who are to form the next Parliament will be selected by the several classes of constituencies in the fol- lowing proportions :-135 English boroughs will return 227 members; nine frisk boroughs, 16 members; 19 Snatch boroughs, 31 members; eight Welsh boroughs, 11 members; 40 English counties, 233 members; 32 Irish counties, 85 members; 29 Scotch counties, 39 members;. 12 Welsh coun- ties, 19 members; and six Universities, 9 members. AU the constituencies are arranged in single-member, areas with the exception of the following, which will continue to return two 'members each under the old system of dual voting:—City of feendon, Oxford Unieersity, Cambridge University, Dublin University; Bath, Blackburn, Bolton, Brighton, Derby, Devonport, Halifax, Ipswich; Leicester, Newcastle-on-Tyne, Northampton, Norwich, Oldham, Plymouth, Preston, Ports- mouth, Southampton, Stockport, Sunderland, York, Cork, Dundee. and Merthyr Tydvil. Ma. GOSCHEN AT EDINBURGEL—Mr. Goschen spoke at Edinburgh On Saturday. He said that regarding Ireland Lord Salisbury was not quite so clear as he should be. nor as deeisive as the country had a right to expect him to be. (Cheers, and "Go between.') Did Lord Salisbury hope that the solution of the Irish difficulty waste be found in the direction of federation, and that Ireland was to that extent to be separated from the United Kingdom n As to local reforms, he (Mr. Goschen) would prefer to sae them carried out according to the methods which had characterised the former reforms of the Liberal party. Speaking of drink, be said he believed if Sir Wilfrid Lawson's movement were capable of being carried to an end, it would de more to empty our workhouses than all the schemes of Mr. Jesse Collings. Sir Wilfrid Lawson's scheme might by Utopian, but they might depend upon it that it WAS by temperance, by education, ani by religiou—(hear, hear, and cheers)— that we should do more to reduce the hideous state of things existing in our great cities than by any other system of municipal socialism—(cheers)—or thh compulsory pur- chase of allotments of land by corporations. GRIRVANCES.—The Indian delegates who have come to this country to lay their grievances before the elec- tors have issued an address on behalf of the people of India. They ask the electors to support snob a change as shall recognise the people of Indie as loyal subjects of the great British Empire and give them the privileges of free citizens). On the question of aggression, the delegates plead that the policy of meeting the enemy far away from the frontier, though it may dazzle some by its magnificence, is not the path of ascertained safety, which they consider is that the Indian Empire should be defended from within its borders, and remain independent of the fluctuations of a foreign policy in the shaping of which it has no share. They ask for a commission of inquiry into Indian affairs as soon as the new Parliament meets, a consideration of reforms on the lines of Mr. Bright's proposals in 1858, a changed military policy whereby the extreme costliness of Indian military ad- ministration may be reduced, and a practical enforcement of those principles of equal rights and equal justice for all races, creeds, and classes so often insisted on by Enrrlish statesmen and so generally ignored by their rulers in India. Mn. HERBERT GLADSTONE ON IRELAND.—Mr. Herbert Gladstone, speaking in West Leeds, on Monday, for which division he is a candidate, referred to the liberality that was boasted in Lord Salisbury's speech as accounted for by fright at Mr. Chamberlain and the hope to catch the Whigs. He reverted to his speech at Leeds in July on the question of Ireland, saying that it was the central question of the day and would not be put aside. On the former occasion he charged the Conservative party with making a compact with Mr. Parnell, and in thus describing what took place he was wrong, but he did the Tory party no injustice, because nothing he said was untrue. lie supported this assertion by referring to the attitude of the Conservative party towards the Nationalist members. Lord Salisbury did not advise his party on this burning question of the day because he was between the devil and the deep sea. He was depend- ant upon Mr. Parnell for order is Ireland, and he dare not openly support his programme because he would lose the support of a large lection of the Conservative party. What was to be done? The present system of Government in Ireland had no longer a defender. All parties were prac- tically united in advocating the abolition of the Lord Lieutenancy, and that local government ought to he thoroughly reformed. The Government of Ireland must be reconstructed from top to bottom. CAIIDINAL MANNING AND CATHOLIC VOTERS.—Cardinal Manning contributes to the Dublin Review an article " How shall Catholics vote at the coming general election ? " His eminence thinks that no goodwill can be expected from Irish Catholics to the Orange garrison, or' to Dublin Castle, or to the English Government, which for 300 years perse- cuted, pillaged, and oppressed them; but he enforces the duty on every Catholic to bear goodwill to the civil order, which is of divine origin. The English constitution is a Catholic inheritance, and he defends the Crown, Lords, and Commons. As to disestablishment. Catholics would be glad by spiritual action to gather the British people into their fold, but they cannot unite with men believing little or nothing to destroy what remains of Christian belief in the country. His Eminence urges that Catholics must strive at whatever cost to preserve England from an irrelieions system of education, and enforces the importance of the housing of the poor, a change in the land laws, and the enactment of local option. Of all these measures the say- ing of the Christian education of the people is the most vital, and demands the promptest treatment, and on the answer of candidates as to whether they will endeavour to place voluntary schools on an equality with Board schools, and to appoint a Rival Commission to review the present state of education, the Catholic vote should be decided.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present— the Rev. G. F. Roberts f(chairman), Messrs. Derbyshire, Ap- pleton, Brown, Bonrretl, Mackie, Jolley, Rlackhurst, Green- ing, Ratcliffe, John Houghton, William Houghton, Hunt, Foster, Balbarry, Broadbent, Owen, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk.) RELIEVING OFFICERS AND REGISTRATION. On the usual cheques being submitted to the Board, Mr. Avemevon called attention to charges of £3 13s 6d by the relieving officers, Messrs. Harbourne and Garnett, being 103 6d per day each for attendance at the recent Revision Court for the borough of Warrington. He (Mr. Appleton) thought these sums were rather large, and he noticed that Mr. Caldwell, the relieving officer for Newton, did not make any charges for attending Revision Courts.—The 'CLERK said that Warrington was a borough and revision was for Parliamentary and municipal purposes.—Mr. DAREYSHIRE asked if these were legal charges; he was not aware that the cost of the revision of voters came out of the poor rate.— The CLERK: Oh yes. The question whether the 'relieving officers were entitled to make these charges was really one for the auditor.—Mr. Beacsetturtsr : What are the duties performed ?—The CLERK said the officers attended upon the barrister and supplied him with such information as he might require. He knew there was a feeling on the part of the auditor that it was part of the officers' duty; but it was purely a matter between the auditor and them.—Mr. DAR- DISTURB thought 10s 6d for each attendance was a rather large amount —The CLERIC.: Does the barrister allow it? —Mr. Breoween Yes.—The CLERK: Then you must pay it. —The accounts were then passed. SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.—APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER. At a meeting of the above committee held on the 13th October, the Rev. G. F. Roberts in the chair. The com- mittee having considered the applications for the office of the Medical Officer for the schools decide to recommend to the Board the appointment of Dr. Fox, subject to approval by the Local Government Board. The committee recom- mended that the thanks of the Guardians 'be given to Dr. Joseph for accepting the medical defies at the schools pend- ing the proposed new appointment of medical officer, and for the excellent attention given by him to such duties, and furthet that Dr. Joseph be requested to present an account for the services rendered to the period of the confirmation by the Local Government Board of the new appointment recommended. An interesting letter by John Brady, mili- tary band boy, aged 16, and formerly a pupil of Mr. Mines at the Union Schools, and written from Etschowe, Zulu. land, on the 6th ult was read, and the committee were par- ticularly pleased with Brady's penmanship aud composition. —The CHAIRMAN moved the confirmation of these minutes with the exception of the clause referring to the appoint- ment of a medical officer. That matter had been before the committee on the previous day, and the result of their deliberations was that they unanimously appointed Dr. Fox to the position of medical officer at the schools. The com- mittee thought it unnecessary and unadvisable in their own interests to mention the names of the other candidates for the post. But the reason why he now excepted the clause referring to the appointment of Dr. Fox, was that he had just received a note from that gentleman to say that since he sent in his application for the post of medical officer of the schools he had made inquiries respecting the duties, and after considering the matter carefully over he begged to withdraw his name as the salary was inadequate to the duties to be performeg.—Mr. GREENING seconded the pro- posal of the Chairman.—Dr. MACKIE said he had taken it for granted that the appointment of medical officer would be considered that morning. He should like to know whether it was wialin the province of the committee to appoint or even to recommend an officer.—Mr. GREENING thought that the very fact of the recommeedation being on the minutes answered Dr. Mackie's queetion.—Dr. MACKIE: I want to know whether it is within the powers of the committee to do it.—Mr. BROADBENT: It is to recom. mend.—Mr. BLACKHURST thought the usual way in the ap- pointment of officials was for the Board to decide, so that every member of the Board might have the opporthnity of proposing a candidate. He had not been at the previous meeting when the salary was fixed, but he thought that. considering the duties, £2O was too little. ,It would have been much wiser to have fixed it at something like £3O, seeing that the old officer received £3s.—The CHAIRMAN: A good many gentlemen then present thought the same, but they were in a minority.—Mr. BRaWN had been under the impression that the appointment was te be made that day.—The CLERK said it had been agreed to leave the selec- tion to the committee. He suggested that the whole sub- ject be referred back.—Mr. Boower wished to know if there had been any other applicants. If there were they had a right to know, so that they might make the appointment that day. (steer, hear.)—Dr. MACKIE hoped that the names of the applicants would be mentioned, and the elec- tion allowed lobe made.—Mr. GREENING suggested that the minutes be passed as proposed. and then the election of a . medical officer proceeded with. He maintained that the" committee had done nothing but of the ordinary course.— Mr. BLACKHURST asked that the resolution stating that the selection be left to the committee should be read.—The CLERK said that had been decided more in the way of con- versation than by a particular resolution.—Mr. APPLETON thought Dr. Fox should have considered before he made his application whether the salary was sufficient or not. He could not understand such a proceeding.—Mr. BROADBENT thought it had been shown that the action of the committee was perfectly regular; if there had been-any irregularity it had been on the part of Dr. Fox. Of course, it was presumed that before a gentleman applied for a certain office he took care to ascertain not only the salary, bat also what the duties were. He (Mr. Broadbent) also re- ferred in complimentary terms to the manner in which Dr. Joseph had discharged his duties at the school since Dr. Spinks' retieement.—Dr. MACKIE said they had not yet been told who the applicants were, and therefore they were speak- ing is the dark.—The CHAIRMAN said there had been only two applications, one being from Dr. Fox and the other from Dr. Jack.—Dr. MACKIE: Both excellent men.—Mr. DARBY- SHIRE thought the appointment ought to be settled that day.—The minutes with the exception of the clause refer- ring to the appointment of Dr. Fox were then passed —Mr. lONNELL proposed that Dr. Jack be app tinted medical offi- cer at Padgate schools.—Mr. DeleneentnE seconded this proposal. He said he did not place much confidence ill the remarks that had been made about the salary being too small. So far as be could see the salary Was sufficient, but if it were found that it was too small he was sere tke Board would increase it when the time carne.—Mr. BROADEONT said he still thought the salary offered toe low. 'lire very fact that Dr. Joseph had visited the schools three days a week and sometimes had children at his surgery would show them that £2O a year was not much remuneration. What they had to do, however, was to loyally carry out the decisions of the majority of that Board. (Hear, hear.) He as a member of the committee could say that the committee were very well satisfied with the two applications that were made, and they were quite unanimous in the opinion that either one or other of the two gentlemen who applied was quite capable of performing the duties. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. FOSTER pointed out thet Dr. Jack had been appointed Dr. Spink's deputy medical officer at the Wotkhouse, while it bad been decided by the Board that it was not desirable to have the Same medical officer at both establishments. (Hear, hear.)—The CHAIRMAN thought Dr. Jame might be appointed on the under- standing that he resigned his appointment as deputy at the Workhouse.—Mr. JOLLEY said that on that understanding he would support the resolution. He hoped the salary would soon be raised, as it was quite inadequate.—Mr. GREENING thoteeht it weld he necessary that Dr. Jock should cease to be deputy at the Workhouse it he was appointed medical officer at the schools.—Mr. APPLETON quite approved of the appointment of, Dr. Jack.—Dr. MACKIE asked if there was any illegality in a medical officer holding the two offices.— Mr. BLACKTIURST did not think there was anything of the kind in the consolidated order.—The CLERK said there was no legal difficulty in the way, but they had made it a com- plaint against' Dr. Spinits that in their experience the arrangement of the two efficesbe ng united ought not to becon- tinuecl, and he had by the direction of the Board pressed that objection on the Local Government BAH, until they finally agreed that the two appointments should not be held by the same person. In this matter they must understand that Dr. Spinks is Dr. Jack, and Dr. Jack Dr. Spinks. One might come to the Workhouse ten times and the other only two times, but they could never tell which would come. He had no doubt that after what had passed Dr. Jack would be quite willing to resign his depntyship.—ls was then agreed to by Mr. Bonnel that the condition that Dr. Jack should, on his appointment to the medical officership of the schools, resign his appointment as Dr. Spinks' deputy at the Work- house, should be added to his proposal, which Was then carried unanimously. sCHOOL FEES —TRE,QUESTION OF FREE EDUCATION. The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been ' allowed in 73 cases, 52 of which were old and 21 new cases. —Mr. BROM moved, and Mr. GREENING seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Dr. MACKIE asked if there was likely to be any return at an eerlv date as to the number and cost of the school fees allowed for the last six or twelve months. They were all aware of the deep interest that was being taken in the subject at the present time, and the prob- able effect of any information they might have would be to bring the public mind to better understand the propriety, which he stroneiy believed in, of entirely abolishing school fees. The last time the suhject was before them it turned out that they paid no less than £ll9 in school fees, anti that went a long way in support of the proposition made lately in ibis town bye very eminent member of one of the political parties, that the time was rapidly corning when the whole of the fees ehocid be abolished altogether. He JDr. Mackie) should lie very glad. if there was an authentic report given some day somis At the last meeting of the committee he was, at there was no less than 90 cases before them. Poe.- women and children had to come and beg for school fees from the committee. If they could get rid of that process he was sure the whole of the Guardians would be delighted indeed. (Rear, bear.) If they could get any authentic particulars he was sure they would be worth giving, and they would perhaps set a good ex imple to other Boards of Guardians—The CillennipN suggested that Dr. Mackie should move that ouch a re/tun should made Dr. Macrae Moved to that effect, and expressed a hope that the Town Cauneil would follow it up. FYLDE SHIRE HORSES.—That celebrated brood mare by Honest Tom, dam of Royal Stamp, and Thistlexern (which have stood so well up in the London shows) and other prtzeiwinners, have been purchased at a high figure by a noted Yorkshire horse breeder from Mrs. Hull and Sons, farmers, Thistleton, in the Fylde. THE WHEAT CROP or 1885.—Sir J. B. Lawes writes as follows it very rarely that the weathers has been more favourable than that which we have had this year for the ripening and harvesting of the, wheat crop of the country. In writing a few years ago on the influ- ence of climate upon our wheat crops, we pointed out that in those years in which the yield of wheat was un- usually large, one of the peculiar characteristics of the .climate was the steady and progressive increase in the temperature during the whole period of the growth of the crop. . _ _ . . . .

Loan SIIDELEY'S LABommas.-Lord Sudeley, having re- ceived a petition from the working men on his Gregynog estate asking that all industrious and thrifty persons might have sufficient land to keep a cow, replied that he already had 126 holdings on that estate under 45 acres. He had always been in favour of granting to his labour- ers one-quarter or half an acre of land under proper con- ditions. It was not, of course, possible in every case to give sufficient pasture to keep a cow, as'Aue regard must be paid to the conditions and requirements of the neigh- bouring farms, but, so far as he was concerned, he could only say that he should be extremely pleased to see no exception to the rule. RICE MEAL—I notice enquiries are being made with regard to rice meal as a food for various purPoses, and would take this opportunity of pointing out thelvarying quality of this substance. Some of the samples of rice meal found in the market are exceptionally rich, and , form excellent food for stock—more particularly for pigs,—while, on the other hand, a considerable percent- age of the samples of rice meal sold to farmers are of very inferior quality, and often adulterated to such an extent as to render the use of such meals positively dan- gerous. Thus, I have just examined a sample of rice meal imported from Italy, which contains upwards of 150 per cedt, of its weight of ground marble, and I have frequently had occasion to analyse samples which I have found adulterated with 20 to 30 per cent, of gyp- sum and carbonate of lime. I have found samples also to contain nearly 20 per cent, of silica, derived 'partly from the "shudes." It, therefore, behoves farmers, in purchasing rice meal, to be sure that only unadulterated samples of good quality are selected, otherwise I fear their experience of this substance as a food will be far from satisfactory.—Alfred Smet ham, F.C.S., Liverpool. STOP CHEESE-MAKING FOR THE CHWIN.—A North Lan- cashire correspondent of the Agricultural Gazette writes: —"The present and probable prices of cheese are barely profitable to the best makers, and perfectly ruinous to all who unfortunately are so unskilled as to produce in- ferior qualities. The price of butter has not been good during the summer, but it has been gradually creeping up, and it has now reached such a point that the churn will pay better than the cheese-tub. Hence I would ad- vise as many cheese-makers as can possibly do so to be- gin butter-making. I know farmers, as 'a rule, do not like going out of the old ruts,' but the present times will: teach them the fdlly of that kind offtenacity, and the necessity for changing, and changing rapidly, when- ever a more profitable course presents itself. If cheese- makers were to cease now they would free that portion of their dairies for sale in the spring from that unmarket- able and undesirable kind (which,is alike the dread of wholesale and retail dealers) known as late makes' or back ends.' Again, it is evident that at the present time, and all through the season, the cheese market has been overstscked ; this and the depression in trade, and an overstocked labour market, has lessened the consump- tion, and there is little sign of a lift in prices. But if the large majority of English makers stopped now they would largely, lessen the supply for sale in the spring, and this would tend to advance prices. Looking at the matter all round I cannot but conclude that churning, and not cheese-making, for the remainder of the season, ought to be the order of the day. At this season of the year many who send milk by rail, and are under con- tract as to quantity, would be saved the necessity of the expenditure involved in buying fresh calving cows to keep up the quantity of their milk if they were to arrange with farmers whose places were conveniently situated on the route to the railway station to furnish them with their supply. This would greatly equalise matters, and both buyer and seller, in such circum- stances, would be accommodated and benefited; and that mode would also prevent an over supply of butter as well as of cheese."

div.head: ENSILAGE COMMISSION:
div.p: THE ENSILAGE COMMISSION:

The Private Ensilage Commission has presented:a pre- liminary report to the Agricultural Department They say : The Commissioners have, up to the present time, held 1•1 sittings b.n4 examined 38 witnesses, comprising among their number owners and occupiers of landed estates and their agents, tenant farmers, designers and inventors of different forms pf silos, or of different systems of applying the necessary •weights to stacked or ensiled green fodder, chemists, and authors of pamphlets • on:the general subject. Sir John Bennett Lawes, whose • eminent knowlege of all matters relating to the chemistry ` of agriculture, combined with the fact that his published opinions on the process of ensilage have been regarded I as unfavourable to the system, has rendered his evidence , of great value and interest. The Commissioners have by no means desired to exclude unfavourable evidence; ` on the contrary, they have endeavoured to induce some ' of those who were believed to be opposed. to the system to give them the benefit of their opinions, but they have ' so far heard no expression of any decidedly unfavourable views. The evidence tendered has been entirely volun- tary, all witnesses attending at their own expense. The evidence of all those who have practically tested the various-methods of converting green fodder crops into preserved food for animals without putting them through any process of drying, such as is necessary in the making of hay, has, without excention, established their claims to a considerable amount of success; and, although in some cases, the results have been evidently more satisfactory than in others, the advantages which the different opera- tors, one and all, have claimed for their systems seem to show that a nourishing and useful food for animals can be , preserved, independently of any drying process, within wide lines of divergence in the details of the methods adopted. It has been conclusively shown that, by different • degrees of weighting and of expulsion and exclusion of at- • mospheric air from the material stacked or ensiled, differ- ! ent degrees of heat and of consequent chemical change are produced. The degree to which such chemical changes increase or diminish the feeding value of the silage itself or its relative value in comparison to the green crop, is, in the present state of knowledge, in great measure a matter of opinion, and careful feeding experiments con- ducted with a view to test the exact effect of these changes will be highly important to a solution of this question. Silage which has been covered in immediately after cutting, and not again uncovered, has been shown , to retain its colour and freshness although developing small quantities of certain acids indicative of a process of fermentation without any considerable accession of heat. 'Other silage which has been put in at intervals, and from which the air has not been immediately or en- tirely excluded, has undoubtedly developed considerable heat, and in this case the colouring matter of the leaves has been less well preserved. Yet in both cases a use- ful feeding material has been rendered available which, in favourable weather, would have been practically lost if any attempt had been made to convert it into hay. Bearing in mind the importance of economy, the Com- missioners have inquired into the efficiency of various systems of stacking unchaffed green fodder crops with- out drying, by which it has been contended that, with a proper system of pressure, the necessity for a silo can be done away with. The Commissioners are not at present pre l ared to express any opinion upon the economy of any such system, or to compare its advantages with those which are claimed brthe advocates of chaffed and close stored silage; but it seems to be established that a temperature sufficiently high to involve danger of fire ' can be controlled by a proper and efficient system of applying weight to the stack of green fodder. The different systems of applying weight have greatly occupied the attention of the Commissioners, but as the quality of the silage does not appear to be materially affected by this question, it becomes simply one of economy, and may safely, for the present, be left to each operator to d ecide for himself according to the special circumstances affecting the particular locality in which his farm is situated. Some of the best samples chaffed silage have been produeed with pressure not exceeding 70Ib. per superficial foot, but the degree td which weight- ing is necessary or desirable remains to be decided upon the greatest amount of evidence that may become avail'. , able to us. Good results are claimed to have been ob- tained by means of weights varying from 71b. to 3001 b. per superficial foot on the top of the silage. The experi- ence of dairy farmers does not appear to justify the assertion which has been more or less circulated that dairy produce is, in any way, injuriously affected by silage as food; on the contrary, much valuable evidence has been received to show that the feeding of cows with well made silage distinctly improves the yield of milk and cream, and the quality of butter. Where complaints have arisen of milk becoming tainted, the cause has been in our opinion, traceable to its having been in proximity with strong-smelling silage, or with persons who have handled it, rather than to the use of such ma- terial as food. The Commissioners have already heard sufficient evidence to justify them in encouraging the development of the system of storing undried green , fodder crops as a valuable auxiliary to farm practice. In addition to other advantages, the losses, occurring through weather unfavourable for haymaking, may be avoided, and some crops not hitherto grown in this country on account of the impossibility of ripening their seed (such as certain varieties of maize), may probably, be successfully cultivated in certain districts, to the in- crease of our present means of feeding various kinds of live stock on arable or partly arable farms.

there was very little difference indeed. He considered that they were paying nearly two-thirds of it already. If it could be shown that the great part of the costs went in the administration of the law it would go a very long way in strengthening the hands of those who want free education. (Hear, bear.)—Mr. Dannvsurau said be was in favour of the return being made, but be was not so much in favour of free education as some people were. (Hear, hear.) He didn't know what the working classes would want next. They had got short hours, and the school fees of the;r children were given them. In a majority of these cases they won't try to work, and he did not see what more could be done for them. There were other people who were pinched in the bad times, but they would have to pay their rates and for education. He had been convinced from time to time that those who applied to tha committee for school fees had not done their best to save fees. They as much as said Be idle and come here for school fees and we will give them to you." Therefore he was not so much in favour of free education; he thought they would be giving a premium on laciness. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. thrown thought that when the report came they would find that a very large percentage of those who went before the magistrates had their school fees paid.—Mr. GREENING t ; not a large percentage.—Mr. JOLLEY said he might, as a school man- ager, tell them that the school fees paid by the town were not a sixth cart of the school pence. Free education would be a more serious matter than they thought.—Dr. Mackie's Proposal was then agreed to. nu. JOSEPH'S ASSISTANT. A letter was read from Dr. Jeseph asking that his 'brother, Dr. J. F. Joseph, might be appointed his deputy in No. 1 district in place of Dr. Spinks.—This request was acceded to.

• THE WORK OF THE MEDICAL OFFICERS. The CLERK submitted, in accordance with a motion by Mr. Gibson at the previous meeting, a statement showing the work of the medical officers of No. J. district (Dr. Joseph) and No. 2 district (Dr. Spinks). The statement showed that the total number of attendances on the poor by Dr. Joseph was 1,733, as compared with 438 by Dr. Spinks. It was stated that the areas of the two dis- tricts was about the same, and the salaries of the two offi- cers alike.—lt was agreed that en account Of Mr. Gibson's absence the statement should lie on the table. This was all the business 'of public interest.

At Bilston, on Tuesday, John Wildman, miner, was charged with a murderous assault on P.C. Snow. Snow went to arrest the prisoner, who attacked him with a miner's pick. The prisoner was remanded for a week. DISESTABLISHMENT.—The Bishops of Peterborough and St. Albans, speaking at their respective diocesan conferences on Wednesday, referred at sorne length to the disestablish. ment question, both of them urging Churchmen to rally to ! the defence of the Establishment. THE Sr. LOUIS MURDER —Mr. Brooks, headmastdr of the Stockport National Schools, has left for America, to tike steps for the defence of his son, wile is charged with the I murder of Mr. Preller_ Mr. trooks regards the identity of his son as established beyond question. A COOL CUSTOMER.—Thomas Kine, of Manchester, was on Monday charged with burglary at the residence of Mr. Riley, pianoforte maker, Birmingham. He was discovered seated in an armchair, smoking a cigar abstracted from a I box on the sideboard, with his plunder carefully packed for removal by his side. A Fronir WITH POACHERS.—Nine keepers and watch- men in the service of Lord Crewe came upon Id armed poachers on Tuesday night in Crewe park. A desperate fight ensued. Eventually the keepers had to retreat for assistance, and the poachers escaped, leaving a large num- ber of rabbits and a quantity of netting. IMPRISONMENT OF 350 MIKERS.—On Monday nigbt, for abaut eight hours, 350 miners were imprisoned in the Silkstone pit of Messrs. Pope and Pearson, Limited, Al- tais. near Normanton. The crank of the engine broke whirl all the men were at work, and it was not until fate that it was suiEciently repaired to enable the men to be drawn up. AN INDUSTRIAL 1:10)1E BURNT.—At Clerkenwell, on Mon- day; Fredrick William Dunkley, aged 11, was remanded, charged with setting fire to a wood abed beneath the dormi- tory at Islington Industrial Home for Boys, of which he ' was an initiate. The premises were gutted. All the boys were rescued. The prisoner afterwards made a statement implicating himself. MURDEROUS ASSAFLV.—A man named Alfred Hartley Oled in the General Hospital, Birmingham, on Wednesday, from injuries received on Saturday night, when he was at- tacked by four men at Smethwick, near Birmingham, and robbed of his week's wages. He was found lying in an in- sensible condition in the road, but recovered sufficiently to say how his injuries bad been canoed. No arrests have been made. „ e.

1 RESENT MONS TO THE REV.

_ FATHER EENNON. INTE ESTING GATHERING. The Rev. James Lennon, who for the peat 15 years has bad charge of the Catholic Mission in Crow-lane, Exiles- town, was on Monday evening the recipient of handsome testimonials of the respect in which he is held by the con- gregation under hint. The present beautiful chapel, known as St. Mary's and St. John's, was erected abut 20 years ago, and the priest in charge was the Bev. John Lennon, brother of the Rev. James Lennon. The latter gentleman succeeded his brother, who accepted the charge of a mie- tion at Chorley. During the succeeding 15 years the pre- sent pastor has laboured zealously for the cause of Catholicism and the benefit of those under him, and his success has been remarkable. He has endeared himself to the parishioners and congregation by his kindness and geniality on every occasion, and their respect for him is shared by members of other religious denominations. About three months ago the Rev. Father Lennon proceeded to the Continent with the view of recruiting his declining health, and during his absence the congregation and friends de- cided to acccrd him a hearty welcome on his return and at the same time present to him a tangible mark of their ap- preciation of his services. The latter took the form of a handsomely painted testimonial, a purse containing £56, and a splendid dining table centre piece. The gathering was held in the large schoolroom, and there was a crowded and enthusiastic audience. The room had been tastefully decorated for the occasion, and presented a bright and pleasant appearance. Mottoes, such as" Health and happi- ness to our pastor," 4. Welcome home," and " A thousand welcomes," gave appropriate expression to the evidenced feelings of those present. It had heen announced that the Rev. Father Byrne, of Golborne, would preside. but in his ab- sence at the commencment Mr. Jno.Unsworth was elected to preside. He was supported by the Rev. Father Lennon (whose appearance was greeted with three hearty cheers), the Rev. Father John Lennon, of Wellbank, Chorley, Rev. Father Clarke (Croft), Messrs. Macadam (town councillor, Liverpool). Thomas Forster, James Water, M. Reaney, M. Griffin, and John Derbyshire (members of the committee.) The other members of the committee were Messrs. T.Kenny (treasurer), J. Banks, W. Wilkineon, B. Dolan, R. Bart- ley, R. Walmsley. E. Fitzgerald, J. Fitzgerald, E. Col- lins, J. Jordan, P. Dee, P. McMahon, and H. Huckson (secretary.) The proceedimes commenced by the choir, under the leadership of Mr. John Banks, excellently rendering a glee 4. Hail to our priest," during the recital of which the entire audience rose. Mr. James Edge efficiently accompanied on the pianoforte. The piece had been specially composed for the occasion by the Rey. Father Byrne, of Golborne, and the words were as follows : "Rail to our Priest who In triumph advances! Ilonour'd and blessed of B.S. Mary and John; Lovelight divine every feature enhances, Dwelling enshrined likes saint on his throne. God grant thee strength anew, Heaven drop down virtue's dew Daily to aid thy frail flowers to bloom. Bing we our heart's refrain— Heaven will approve the strain ! Vireiceme dear Father, glad welcome home. Wildly our heartstrings are thrilling with devotion, No fitful sound. no 'twill ever abide; Broader and deeper than earth-circling ocean Is our love ot thee, dearest Father and guide. God grant thee strength. &c. Sing, children, sine for the pride of our meeting! Long may his smile like a guiding star Shine o'er the hours of our lives, oh, so fleeting, Lighting the glo sm with a radiance divine. God grant thee el rengtb, Ac. The Chairman regretted the absence of the Rev. Father Byrne, and said they were all aware they had met to wel- come home their pastor, and he hoped they would give him the welcome he deserved. (Applause.) Several friends had been written to asking for the favour of their presence. Dr. Fox, of Warrington, had written apologising for his in- ability to attend, and stating that their gifts to Father Len- non were richly merited, for he had worked zealously and with much self-sacrifice amongst them. (Applause.) He (Dr. Fox) was sure that spontaneous effort among the people during the present bad times would be fully appreciated ny the recipient, and give him pleasure to think that be lived in the hearts of the people. (Applause.) Mr. T. Kenny then sang "Old friends met together," and was accorded hearty applause. The Rev. Father Blake, of Croft, who was warmly re- ceived, said anything he could say in praise of Father Lennon was in their hearts. (Applause) They loved him dearly, and he had joy in sharing their welcome to him. If he was to enumerate the good virtues of Father Leanon, that gentleman would be annoyed, as he (Father Blake) knew his retiring disposition. They. all felt Father Len- non'a goodness when he moved amongst them, attended their sick, and stood by the death bed. Many a soul was praising him that night in heaven, and they all united in that praise. They loved him tenderly, and he (Father Blake) desired to unite with them in wishing him health and strength that God Almighty might enable him to cone tines his good work amongst them. (Cheers.) The Rev. Father Byrne, of Golborne, then entered the room, and was received with loud applause. Miss Kate Holland afterwards nicely sung, "Thy face." The Chairman stated that the next business was the presentation. He then read the testimonial, which was in the following terms e- -4. To the Rev. Father Lennon, Pastor of Bt. Mary's and St. Jelin's Church, Newton-le-Willows. Dear Reverend Father,— We have felt your absence so deeply that we onild not allow you to come home without some expression of web- me and joyous thaekfulness: at your return. You have had our heart- felt sympathy in your sickness, and, we trust, that if not quite restored to health, through our prayers and with the blesssing of God, arm soon may be. We present you with this a 'dress and testimonial as a token of our esteem and admiration of your ckaracter, and of our appreciation of your zealous and earnest labours on our behalf in the past. You never ceased urging and exhorting us to per.evere in the path of virtue, the love of God, and the precbiee of our religion. You never hesi- tated to tell us of our faults with a cionscientlous sense of your duty as a true priest. Your loving care for our little r nes end your anxiety for their education, spletoal and temporal, touches us specially. For our amusement you have g•ven us eommodlons bail in which to assemble when we wish. and furnished suitably for our entertainment.. besides many other expenses for the sebools and otherwise, which you have gener- ously taken upon yonrself. Again, dear reverend father, we. the parents. youth, and children of your missmn, express our loving gratitude for all you have eM- e for us, and ask you t accept this address and accompanying purse of geld, and in the future may Alm'ghty God give You health and strength to continue your latonrs amiegs-, us is the earnest prayer of• your patishionera. the Cathodes of Eariestown and Newton- le-Willows. Signed on their behalf. J Uneworth, chairman, Robert liacksn, cemetery. Thomas Kenny. treasurer. St. Mary's and Bt. Jehu'a (Mho ic Hall. Newton-le-Willows, October 12th, 1885." (Cheers.) The address is surrounded by a beautiful floral border with a design of Our Blesard Lady, beneath which are the words on a scroll. " Suffer little children to oome unto Me, and forbid them not." It was enclosed in a handsome frame' and had been prepared by Mr. J. A. Fiaigan, of 174 South Castle-street, Liverpool. . Mr. Michael Griffin, one of the oldest members of the congregation, handed the testimonial an 4 beauti, al beaded purse, containing £56, to Father Lennon. In doing so he alluded to the pleaeieg duty which he performed, he said on behalf of the whole congregation. (Cheers.) . The school children then presented a splendid silver epergne, or dining table centre piece, to Father Lennon. The following address, by which it was accompanied, was nicely read by Miss Katie Lackey, one of the school chil- dren : ~Wewton-le-Willews, 12th October, 1885.—Dear Rev. Father, —We. the little children of your echo -I, are here to-night to wish you from our Ilea ts a weloome home. We cannot tell you how we have missed you day by day, and with what joy we welcome your return to us. But though we could not see you as we used to do, we never for lot to mention your name in our miming or evening prayers. As a email token of our great love for You, arid joy at seeing you °nee again, we beg of you. dear Reverend Father, to accept cur little present. it is small, but our hearts are big, and with loving grateful hearts we beg to offer it to you. Again wishing you a hearty wel- come and asking your blesiug. we remain, dear Reverend Father, the children of St. lieu's and Et. John's School." The Rev. Father Lennon, on rising to acknowledge the gifts, was received with profs need applause. After observ- ing that it was a novel position for him to occupy in being the recipient of such a mark of favour as they had given him, he proceeded to say that ha had never expected such a recognition of his services. He desired to be candid with them. He had always flattered himself, and he thought he would go to his grave with the noble boast that he had served in the sacred ministry for—he did not know how many years-22 years at present—and he had received no other human reward than the heartfelt thanks of a grateful congregation, and, he hoped, the bleasing of God. When he left England. if he had had the slightest idea that they intended to make the generous offer they had done on his return he would have left strict injunctions that it should be nipped in the bud, but he never dreamed of such a thing. But he appreciated their offering, and thought there might be occasionally little heart-burnings when he looked upon their gifts as a testimony that he had the affection and confidence of the Catholics of that parish. (Applause.) He must eincerely and affectionately thank them for that mark of confidence and appreciation of his services. He bad been in their midst for 15 years. and he conld not help feeling they had done a good work. They had finished a gteat work, in completing the church with its spire and tower ^, they had built schools, they had a respectable hall, enlarged house and school house. All that work, he thanked God, hid not only been done, but it had honourably been paid for—(gheers)—and it had been done at no small cora, for they had actually expended between £l,OOO and £5,000 in those great works. He, could not have done it himself, but it had been done with their help and generosity. They had a church and surroundings of which they were not ashamed—(hear, hear)-1 schoolroom and priests' house, which, if they did not make them respected, made them at least respectable, and they had not only those buildings, but they bad a congregation, and it bad been his boast—though he did not want to flatter them—that he would not give the Newton congregation for any other congregation in the wholeedlocese of Liverpool. (Cheers) It might be said by some that they were praising him and that he was praising them, but that was not Co. Most of them would acknowledge that he had never been afraid of sneaking the truth, when it was necessary, and sometimes when it was not necessary. (Laughter.) He urged upon them that the work of edu- cation had not been neglected in the parish, and said they had good useful schools, second to none in usefulness, per- haps not the best in ornament, but they were approved not

only by ordinary visitors, but by her Majesty's inspectors, and they were not only provided with everything that was necessary, but with children, who, like the conere.ration, were second to none; if they were not the first in the dio- cese of Liverpool. (Applause.) The schools had been spoken of very highly by the Government inspectors in the Government reports, end showed that the, were not go- ing backwards, ,but advancing steadily in the educational position of the country. He again thanked them for their kind gift and said be did not intend to use the gold they had given him for his own personal benefit, but to devote it towards founding a fund for the education of students in the Christian ministry at a college in France, where he had been treated with the greatest kindness and cordiality, and where during his stay amongst them they had done every- thing to make him happy and comfortable. He was sure they would approve of that disposition of their kind offer- ing to him. (Applause.) Whatever he had done had been done for their service and interest, spiritual and tem- poral, and he had rejoiced to see them prosper in both. (Ap- plause.) He hoped the same spirit of kindliness and love would animate them in future years, and as long as God gave him strength to remain in their midst—it would never be of his own accord, but only when he felt that 0* reli- gion suffered at his hands that he would anything else but hope that nothing but death would separate him from them. (Loud applauee.) The Rev. John Lennon, of Chorley, briefly alluded to his early connection with the formation of the mission, and said he was proud that his brother had merited their good will. (Applause.) Mr. John Banks then sang" I don't know von," which was warmly encored, and he gave " Good night." Ad- dresses were afterwards given by the Revs. Father Byrne (Golborne), and Sowden (Chorley), the proceedings, which bad been of a very enjoyable character threughout, con- cluding with a hearty and deserve) vote of thanks to the chairman.

div.head: MR. McMINNIES, M.P.. ON PRIMITIVE
div.p: MR. McMINNIES, M.P.. ON PRIMITIVE
METHODISM.

.On Monday ever;;W-Illr:-M-c-ii-nnies, M.P. for the borough, took the chair at a fruit banquet held in connec- tion with the harvest festival at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, ia Legla-street, Warrington. There was a large at- tendance. Having been introduced by the Rev. J. Calvert, pastc r, The CIIMIRMAN, who was received with applause, said that be was very grateful to the audience for the reception that they had given him. He supposed that they were simply there in connection with the bounties of Providence through the harvest which had just been gathered in. They bad from Providence every year a very large increase of their worldly subsistence and for their sustenance. Many millions of pounds sterling came from the earth every year for the maintenance of God's creatures. He only wished that they could get as. much out of the soil of the land as God Almighty had intended that they should do. Bat until the manufacture of food was conducted in the same way as other smaller manufactures were conducted they should never get from God the "earth and the fulness thereof." He was very glad to meet them there that night. It had so happened that for several years he had not met them as frequently as he used to do. He did not exactly know wily, bat such was the case. In former days he used to meet them often and he always did so with pleasure. (Hear, hear.) He had had for many years a particular interest in that society, which was one of the youngest of the free churches of this country. He supposed that it was not more than seventy years ago since the Primitive Methodist Society was formed, and it had grown until at the present time it occupied at least the third place amongst the free churches. There was a time when it was everywhere spoken against, and nowhere more spoken against than in Warrington. Some of their earliest preachers were mobbed, insulted, and persecuted out of the place—(hear, hear)—and one of the most emi- nent of them was interfered with by the then only magis- trate in the town, who went into the house where he was preaching, demanded his license, and threatened to enforce the penalties of the law. Well, they had more than one magistrate in Warrington now, but there was not one—nor any man having authority—who would dare to so oppose any member of that society, or any of the Christian society. Their society was a singular instance of the ad- vancement of the last seventy years. (Hear, hear.) He must exprese the sincere desire that the society might con. tinue to progress as it bad done, and he hoped that the besetting sin of the churches would never hinder their pro- gress—he meant by the besetting sin a certain want of union and forbearance one towards another which they sometimes found. Let them be kindly and forbearing one towards another. (Applause.) The programme for the evening was than proceeded with. Hymns were sung by the choir, and, among others, the fol- lowing gentlemen gave short and appreciative addresses, :—Messrs. Taylor, Ryder (Widnes), Pillinger, and Owen (Widnes.) At intervals young lady members of the con- gregation handed round fruit and other edibles, not because, as the Chairman observed, like Oliver Twist, those present asked for them, but because they were requested to partake of the good things. The chapel had been very prettily adorned with harvest tokens, perhaps rather too profusely so, bat the general appearance was attractive and chaste. On the Sunday harvest thanksgiving services were held. when the Rev. J. Calvert preached to large congrega- tions.

- Two horses, the property of a farmer named Manning, living near Ardee, county Louth, were found dead on Mon- day, having during the night been maliciously stabbed. At Dunmanway, county Cork, Petty Sessions, on Mon- , day. Patrick Cullinane was returned for trial, for boycott- ing and preventing people from doing what they had a legal right to do, under the Conspiracy and Protection of Pro-, perty Act. REFUSAL TO PAY RENT.—On Saturday 300 of the tenants on the Kikenny Estate of the Earl of Bessborough signed a declaration that they would not pay the half-year's rent now due unless they obtained a reduction of 30 per cent. His lordship was waited upon by a deputation, and having bes_n informed of the resolve of his tenants, replied that he would not accede to their request, but would deal with each case on its merits. On Monday morning Constable Glancy arrested John Oronan and Thomas Cronan on the charge of oomplicity in the murder of the father of the first-named. The de- ceased and his son John lived in a house close to the main street, and on Sunday the house was closed all day. On tlee police entering they found the decessed with shocking wounds on the head. The deceased was about 70 years old, and a day or two previously had withdrawn about £2O from the bank. NATIONAL LEAGUERS TO BE PROSECUTED.—The Central News Cork correspondent telegraphs :—The Government are about to prosecute the Middleton Branch of the National League for conspiracy. At last Sunday's meet- ing the members, despite the caution of their rev, president, passed a resolution to morally chastise Denied Humphreys with a view to compelling him to reinstate a tenant evicted for non-payment of two years' rent. Since then shop- keepers in the town and a news agent having been in receipt of threatening notices, have discontinued sopplying Mr. Humphreys with goods they were accustomed to sell to him. SKIRMISH BETWEEN POLICE AND MOONLIGHTERS. About midnight on Sunday a party of mounted and armed men surrounded Lord Healey's mansion, about two miles from Killarney, where Mr. S. M. Hussey, agent to Lord Kenmare, Lord Headley, Mr. Herbert, and other Irish land- lords are residing. Police sentries were on duty around the house. Several shots were fired at the sentries, and the fire was briskly returned by, the police. After several ex- changes the midnight party made off, none of the police baying been injured. fen arrests have been made. Mr. Hussey went into Killarney on Monday morning without any protection. THE SHIPPING OF EMERGENCY CATTLE.—A. meeting of

the shareholders of the Cork Steam Packet Company Was held on Saturday, to consider the representation from the Cattle Trade Association and ether bodies in reference to the shipping of emergency cattle. The chairman, Captain Lyons, presided. Both deputations having been fully heard, the shareholders considered in private what course they would adopt. A ballot was taken. There were 12,612 shares represented in the voting. Of these 11,108 were cast in favour of receiving all cattle of the Loyalist Defence Union. The cattle dealers' deputation were then informed of the ' decision of the shareholders, and, both parties having ex- pressed regret at the strained relations which had been en- gendered, the deputation retired, expressing their determina- tion to carry out their resolve not to send any cattle by the ships of the Cork Steam Packet Comp my. It is etated that the next phase will be the organisatioa of a strike amongst ' the crews of the company's steamers against serving in vessels carrying boycotted cattle.—The Cattle Trade Asso- ciation sent a special train at one o'clock on Monday morn- ing laden with cattle for Waterford, where they would be shipped via Milford. for different English markets. Another train followed at seven o'clock, and arrangements have been made for others during the week.
