SANKEY V. PENKETH.—These clubs met for the first time

- - this season on the ground of the latter on Saturday. Con- siderable interest prevailed and a large number of specta- tors witnessed the match. The home captain won the toss and elected to play against the wind. Asburst for the visitors set the ball in motion about 3-30. Immediately
after the start a scrimmage was formed ia the home 25, when Jefferson., pissed to Barton, who was soon "on the

go," and was within an ace" of scoring when he was brought to grass by Hughes. Another scrimmage here took place, when the home team made a determined attack on their opponents' territory. and Whittle picking up cleared all except Caldwell (the goalkeeper), who tackled him . .
finely. Play continued in Mid-field for a short period when Barton gained possession of the leather and passed to Ash- horst, who succeeded in grounding the ball behind the home
goal. me, amid applause. The same player took the plaoe but owing to the strong wind he failed to improve on the

point. For the rest of the first half the visitors pressed their opponents, forcing them to save three times in quick succession. When ends were changed it was thought that the home team would assume the aggressive, but the visi- tors played a good defensive game. After the ball had been re-started the home team pressed the visitors, but Barton re- lieved by a grand run to centre, but was then pushed in touch. From the line up Hamville passed to Hughes who looked like scoring, when his career was checked by Black- ledge. Here another pack was formed and W. Barton now showed a fine piece of dribbling. Nothing more worthy of notice occurred up to the call of time, when the visitors after a hard-fought game were declared the winners by 1 try and 3 minors to 1 minor. For the visitors Jefferson, Barton, Blackledge and W. Barton played well, whilst for the home team Whittle (a well-known Widnes player) was very con- spicuous.

WIGAN V. RUNCORN.—This match was decided on Satur- day at Wigan, when a very large number of persons wit- nessed a capital game. A strong wind was blowing almost from goal to goal, and the ground, though having a steep incline, was in fair condition; but the distance of the boundary behind the goal line was very limited. Each club put a representative team on the field, the Wigan team being—Anderton, back; Slevin, Smith, and Samuels, three- quarter backs; Morris and Hunter, half backs; Holt (cap- tain), Astley, Cronsbaw, Brayshaw, Wardle, Anderton, Whittle. Ingham, Hayes, forwards; while Runcorn played W. Hughes, hack; Broady. Speakman, and Jo'inson, three- quarter backs; Hughes (captain) and Andrews, half backs; Wright, Joule, Lewis, Dean, Eloffland, Gatley, Barnes, Clarke, and Ligbburn, forwards. The Wigan captain having choice of ends, chose to play down hill and with the wind, which was blowing strongly. Joule set the ball going, when hostilities were located in centre, the ball being gradually worked into the Runcorn half, where Gatley and Joule re- lieved; hut play still cantinued in the visitors' half, and some two or three dead balls were scored by Wigan. The Runcorn forwards played a strong game, and prevented the home players from scoring. Johnson and Speakman both tried for an opening, but their efforts were frustrated. At this juncture Slevin put in a strong run, and got in close quarters to the Runcorn line, but Johnson, assisted by W. Hughes, successfully brought him down, and the danger was averted. Up to half time nothing but minors were scored, the game standing—Wigan, five minor poirus ; Run- corn, one point. Up to this time the Runcorn team had played a hard up hill game, but crossing over they had matters a little more in their favour. Wigan started the ball from the centre, and it was held close up to the visitors' line, when the forwards got away to centre, and a long drop by Broady forced Anderton to kick dead. A similar point was soon after secured by a long kick by Speakman. The home team were now buy defending their lines, Holt, Cronshaw, and A9tley being conspicuous in the work; but being hard pressed the ball was driven in touch in the Wigan quarters, and Broady, being quick in, gave Itughes the ball, and the latter made a determined rush over the line, and gained a meritorious try. Lewis took the place, but without success. From a scrimmage Andrews threaded his way most cleverly through and landed the ball across the line, Lewis converting the try into a goal. Starting off again from centre, runs were made by Johnson. Broady, and Slevin for their respective teams; but the ball falling again into the power of the Runcorn forwards, they got op to the home twenty-five, and while there Speakman got the leather, and with the Wigan pack around sent it flying over the cross bar. From this to the close of the game the home team had to play a hard defensive game, the score at the call of no side being—Runcorn, two goals, one try, four minor points, to Wigan five minor points. The Runcorn forwards played with much cohesion and vigour, which mainly led to the victory. The backs played up well, being very safe, especially when defending their lines. For the Wigan team, Slevin and Morris behind, and Holt, Astley, Cronshaw, and inderton worked hard in the pack. The tour in South Wales has undoubtedly had a bereficial effect upon the Runcorn players. The Welshmen showed them some science, and the Redtaiis, ever willing to learn, took the lesson to heart. They showed by their splendid passing at Wigan of what they are capable. WARRINGTON v. ASICIEAM-IN•FRRNES4 —This match was played at Askham on Saturday last. Unfortunately War- rington were not able to take their beat team, being short of Massey, Buxton, Dillon, and Povey. The Warrington team had a pleasant out, spending an interestin:: hour on the was at Furness Abbey, ultimately reaching Askant, at three o'clock, where there was a large crowd waiting to see what the Warrington lads were like, and the general opinion was, that they were in for a good beating. It must be con- fessed from their appearance that they looked very drowsy after their five hours' long ride. The field on which the contest was to take pl IC3 vras a very rough one. something like a ploughed field. The Askam captain won the toss and elected to play down hill, also having a strong wind,in his favour. Warren set the ball going. and his forwards follow- ing well up, a scrimmage was formed on the Askham 25. On the scrimmage breaking up, the Askham forwards took the ball down the field, Barnes kicking into touch at the Warrington 25. From the line out Rigby got away and dribbled to half-way flag, when Davies picking up made A nice run. After a few scrimmages Thompson for the home team made a short ran and passed to Woodall, who got in a long punt, Jolley touching down. From the kick-off Barnes followed well up, and securing the ball, made a nice dodgy run and passed to Jolley, who was knocked into touch before he could get away. From the line unt, Thompson got hold, and Was making his way, till Warren stopped his progrers, several scrimmages took place, and the bail was again taken to the visitors 25 flag. From the scrimmage the ball was' passed to Tronghtota, who m ide a good run, but was well brought down by Gilbert. The Warrington forwards again , forced their opponents to the half-way flag, where Jolley obtained a free kick, and his forwards following up quickly a scrimmage took place. Hers Warren picked up smartly and passed to Jolley, that player failing to get hold let the Askant men in, who vary q veld v t, ..nsfe,red the play to the Warrington line, Hewitt just saving by kicking the ball into touch. From the line out Warren, by a good dribble, took the ball to half-way hut. the Aslram forwarda again dribbled back again to the visitors' 25. After a rough scrim' mugs or two Gilbert handled the hall and passed to Barnes, who was dodging his oppm-nts nicely when one of the home forwards getting hold if him by the lot threw him heavily to the ground. Ti s necessitated Warrinp,ton play- ing a mau short for the rernaioder of the first half. After several scrimmages Warren got AN'AV and rushed up the field to the Asia= quarters and p4ss,rl to Turner, who nearly got over the line but vas pushed into touch. i Half time was now called. OA routnin,r, Barnes took his place, but was not the help he would have bee/ had he not bee hart. Trougbton kicked off and the hall was carried into touch. From the line out the ball - WAS passed to Barnes,
went

and after several good kicks were put in the ball into touch at the Askam 25. Here Warren got the ball and Passed to Jolley, who missed the catch, and the home for. wards being well up, forced Hewitt to again touch. down. The visitors now began to play with more dash and took the ball down the field, but Macdonald getting possession, m.o. a good run until he was held by Turner. From the scrimmage the visitors put in a splendid dribble to half-way flag. From the Vrow out Slater got the ball and ran in, but was ruled back, the ball haying been passed forward. Here Warren made a good I run and passed to Jolley, who had very hard lines in not I getting over, being brought down by Troughton on the line. After a few scrimmages Macdonald got away, but Gilbert. by a good kick, removed the p:av again to the home quar- ters. After some give and take play the ball went into touch at half-way. From the line out Rigby obtained possession, and clearing all obstacles from his way, ob- tained a try. Turner essayed to kick the goal but was un- successful owing to the high wind. On the ball being brought out the Warrington forwards again dribbled the ball and Speakman getting in his kick sent the hall into touch-in-goal. Troughton kicked off and Barnes made a good run and attempted to drop a goal, the ball being touched down by Askam. On the ball being kicked off Macdonald followed up quick and carried the ball to the visitors' 25, where he was collared by Turner. From the scrimmage Macdonald again broke away, only to be brought down by Speakman. After some good pissing by the War- rington backs, Jolley got off, and made a grand run but was held by Troughton. Time was now called, leaving Warrington victors by 1 try, 2 minors, to Askant 2 minors. For Warrington F. Turner, T. Davies, Hy. Ashton, and Rigby were the pick of the forwards, and of the backs Speakman and Gilbert played a safe game, while Warren played in a most unselfish manner giving his men all the opportunities be could. For Askam, Troughton was the best man and was ably supported by Thompson and Macdonald. Warrington; Hewitt, full back ; Speakman, Barnes, and Jolley, three-quarter backs ; Warren (capt.) and Gilbert, half backs; F. Turner, T Davies, Hy. Ashton, J. Rigby, Hy. Turner, W. lige% J.• Savage, J. Jones, and J. Burgess, forwards; umpire, T. Barnes. Askam : E. Woodall, fall back; Troughton (capt ) Christie, and Lewis, three-quarter backs; Slater and Thompson, half backs; Macdonald, WOodbarn, Anderson, Sharpe, Ellwood, Grey, Wooletul, Hewittson, and Mingins ; 'umpire, Mr. Wilson ; referee, Mr. Barchbank, of Barrow. The visitors, after the match, sat down to a substantial tea which their opponents had kindly provided for them, and they did full justice to everything eatable and drinkable. After several capital speeches from Messrs. Troughton, Warren, Barnes, senior, and March bank, several good songs were given and then the visitors were taken through the works and sow the large blast furnaces at work, which looked grand in the night time, then they were escorted to the station, which they left at half-past eight, arriving at Warrington at half-past eleven, everyone being well pleased with the oat. Manchester opened their fixture list by opposing the Free Wandcrers at Fallowfield. At no time of the game were the Wanderers very dangerous, Manchester winning by one goal, two tries, and six micors, to one try and two minors. _

Liverpool received a visit from Rochdale Harnets, the match ending in a draw, both teams scoring the same points, namely, one goal, one try, and one minor. Durander for Liverpool dropped a splendid goal. That player is rather dangerous in that department. The meeting of Broughton and Broughton Rangers, on the ground of the latter. had for some time evoked a con- siderable anmunt of speculation, the Rangers being greatly fancied after defeating Halifax the previous Saturday. But contrary to expectation Broughton won by two tries and four minors, to five minors. The Rangers were very Lin.- lucky, their full back mulling the ball which enabled Broughton to g•it the two tries. Walton went to Swinton, but were easily defeated by•two goals, four tries, and seven minors, to one try. The Swift. ton Hollis the king of all beasts on its own ground. Warrington took a trip to Askam-in•Furness, calling at Furness Abbey, which was duly inspected. The guide, who had accompanied them, entertained them to a graphic des- cription of the ruins in a manner which was interesting. After a hard and well-contested game Warrington were de- clared the winners by one try and two minors, to two minors. After the match Warrington were right loyally ' entertained by Askarn. Runcorn should be proud of their decisive victory over Wigan, their match taking place on the Wigan ground, The combination of the Runcorn men, was far superior to Wigan. Result at call of time, Runcorn two goals, one try, and four minors, to Wigan fire minors.
WidneA opposed Totttngton on the ground of the former, bat the Chemicals proved too good for Tottington, as they won rather easily by three tries and five minors, to on. miaor. _ _ _ _

Nearly 2,000 persons witnessed the meeting of Bradford and Batley, the ex-holders and holders of the Yorkshire Challenge Cup. After a very exciting game Bradford won by two goals, one try, and fonr minors, to two minors scored by the cup holders. Wakefield Trinity, who are showing splendid form at pre-- ssnt, defeated Manningham after a well-contested game by one goal and six minors, to four minors. Halifax, after their defeat by Broughton Bangers, re- turned the compliment to HudAerscield, winning by one goal, three tries, and seven minors, to five minors.

WAIREINN ON Ale RECALL*—A Plymouth coffee- pondentsays that Sir Charles Warren, who arrived at Ply- mouth from South Atria& On Thursday, stated, in the course of an interview, that he imagines he had been recalled be- cause, although it was not completed, the Government con- aidered his mission successful. He had expel'ed the fili- busters without bloodshed, and as long as the marauding Boers were kept our, the country would remain passive. The native chiefs and Stellaland Boers were most dtsirous ot coming directly under British rule. .

magistracy, he said: "These gentlemen, who possess no representative authority, appoint the chief constable, manage the police, form highway districts, coerce highway boards, decide assessment appeals, manage lunatic asylums, are the principal authority under the Cattle Diseases Act, in regard to weights and measures, and in regard to licences." Sir CHARLES DILKE would reform all this by establishing a purely representative system. He would revert to something approaching the old Saxon system of government by the parish, the hundred, and the county. He would extend the powers of vestries, leaving the vestry to deal with matters purely local; he would establish district boards for the control of affairs of wider scope; and County Boards for what would be regarded as county business. "There would be plenty of work," he says. "for each and all to do with both local and imperial advantage to the realm." There would be an end of irrespons- ible authority; magistrates would cease to have spending powers, except as representa- tives of the ratepayers, and, as rates would be divided between owner and occupier, hiah and low, rich and poor,would have an interest in seeing that the most was got for the money. Lord SairsnuaYtalks plausibly about the. " great principle that all men shall pay according to their ability for the support of local government ;" but, unlike Sir CHARLES DILKE, he does not show how he proposes to bring the principle into operation. It is a favourite doctrine of the Tories that the land should be relieved of its burdens, when, as a matter of fact, it is paying nothing like what it ought to pay in the shape of taxes. If the landowners of the country had kept the bar- gain which they themselves made in 1692 to pay a genuine 4.5. in the pound as a land tax. they would now be paying as much as would meet the expenses of the army and navy year by year, with a few millions besid- towards reducing the National Debt. The landed aristocracy have not only defrauded the nation by evading a just imposition of the land tax—they have robbed the poor of thousands and tens of thousands of common lands. What has Lord SALISIIPRY to say as to restitution in these cases ? Not a word But Sir CHARLES DILKE suggests that reor- ganised vestries should have power given them to protect parish greens, and roadside waste and open spaces, and to compel the I restitution of charity endowments and corn- mon rights which have been illegally appro- priated. Property owners would be allowed fair play, and not as at present unfair play. There would be an end to the system of plurality of votes, whilst voting by ballot would be the rule. The County Boards would deal with such matters as highroads, bridges, lunatic asylums, and prisons. There would be no such difficulty as that which has cropped up in connection with the re-building of Pen- wortham Bridge. in which case the Warring- ton Board of Guardians are being sent from pillar to post by way of ascertaining some thing as to the tax which is being imposed upon them. The County Board would be responsible to their constituents—the rate- payers—and if the members of it did not give a good account of their stewardship they would be dismissed without a blessing. Nor would there be the dissatisfaction which at present exists as to the outcome of the meddle and muddle which the Tories made when previously in office by introducing a wretched system of centralisation in the management of prisons. If anything went wrong, either in parish, district, or county, there woulo be a speedy and an efficient remedy. because each authority would be under the control of those who had to find the ways and means All this is on the assumption that the reform of local govern- ment is thorough; but is it likely that the Tcries, if they get the chance, will make it thorough ? Will they not be too anxious about vested interests to go to the root of the matter ? Will they not be afraid of inter- fering with the power and privileges of their chief supporters ? Will they venture to pave the way for local authorities assisting in ex- periments for establishing peasant proprie- tors ? Will they dare, in view of the pub- licans' vote, to provide a scheme of local option ? These are questions which electors throughout the kingdom would do well to consider. And, coming nearer home, we would ask whether the Tory candidates in South Lancashire and Mid-Cheshire are as likely as the Liberal candidates to support the radical changes which are required ? Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD, as the Liberal can- didate for Warrington, has shown himself ,familiar with the problems of local govern- ment reform ; but as for Sir GILBERT GREENALL, these problems would seem to be beyond his reach ; he cannot, judging from what we see and hear of him, get beyond the preservation of self. fish, and game.

MACKIE has a strong opinion on this subject, and we are glad to see that at the meeting, on Wednesday last, at the Warrington Board of Guardians, he moved for a return of the fees allowed during the past twelve months At the last meeting of the School Fees Committee he attended "we had," he says, " ninety cases before us of women and sometimes their children, begging for school fees." We would hsk if this is not a state of things which calls loudly for a remedy ? These people, it should be re- membered, are not paupers; if they were getting relief, they would not be entitled to apply for remission of school fees; but they are subject to humiliation—they are being pauperised—by having to go begging in this way. And this is only one phase of the evil ; there were "absolutely 380 cases before the magistrates last year " a statement which, simple as it is, is an exceedingly sad one in its suggestiveness. Apart from the harrying of parents, it would be interesting to know how much of the time of the magis- trates was occupied in trying these cases, how much the prosecutions cost the com- munity, and—for the especial benefit of Mr. CARLETON—how many children these parents had tmong them who were absent from school because of the non-payment of school fees.

SIR RICHARD CROSS WaS On Saturday in- vited to "become a candidate in the Con- servative interest to represent the new constituency of the Division of Newton in the new Parliament," and he accepted the invitation. It was commonly understood that he had selected the Newton Division rather than that the Division had selected him ; , but Sir RICHARD would have us believe that ; he is as coy as "sweet sixteen "; and, further, that he has become suddenly enamoured of ' that sound Radical principle—full representa tion of the people. He was asked some time ago if he would come forward as a candidate, but he says—"l replied if I consented it would be when I had seen that the people in their full representative character unani- mously made me their choice." How ex- ceedingly shy, and what a stickler for the Caucus! But who are "the people" in this case? Are we to understarkd that the gen- tlemen assembled in the Newton Town Hall on Saturday were representatives of "the people" as a whole; or would it not be more "germane to the matter" to say that they represented that section of the people known as Conservatives? It is not long since Sir RICHARD CROSS was engaged with other obstructionists in doing all he could to prevent certain of "the people" having a vote at all ; but now that they have shown themselves too strong for him he would wish them "good morrow," and speak of them as his friends. But " the people" will have negard to deeds, not words; and if they look to their own interests they will leave their enemies outside the doors of St. Stephens. The Home Secretary, while himself yielding to the Radical principle which is involved in the Caucus, professes to wonder how it is that so many people think they are Radicals —just as he might wonder how it is that s 2 many people think they stand on their feet and not on their heads ; and he then pro- ceeds to talk about the Conservative princi- ples that are "thrashed out." "Played out" would have been a better phtase, for there are no such goods in the political market now-a days as " Conservative principles." Lord SALISBURY began by denouncing Mr. DISRAELI for deserting "Conservative prin- ciples," and he has lived to " better the in- struction." Sir RICHARD CROSS takes his cue from Lord SALISBURY; and it is too much, of course, to expect him to do any- thing original either in the way of standing by old principles or providing new ones. But, perhaps. we are going too far; for the Home Secretary lets it be understood that he intends to see that no harm shall come to the empire, " for the fall of the empire would tell sooner upon our working-men than upon anybody else." How good of him to offer himself as a buttress I It used to be said that if the sky were to fall all the larks would be caught ; but the fall of the empire is a different thing; Sir RICHARD CROSS tells us it would be no lark to working-men. He should know ; he is a Home Secretary, and has doubtless had experience of this sort of thing. Not long since a noble lord of the Lord GERARD type—who could thank God that he never was a Radical—threatened his labourers to sell off and leave the country if they troubled him as they had done for higher wages. This threat was terrible ; and one of them begged of him if he did go away not to take the land with him. How thank- ful we ought to be that we have GERARDS and CROSSES, and crosses between them, to take care of us. Our duty is clear ; we must send Sir RICHARD CROSS to Parliament, and save the empire.

, SAMARITAN LODGE, WIDNES —The members of this lodge of Good Templar* held their weekly session on Mon- day, tiro. Mackin, W.C.T., presiding. There was a fair at- tendance. After the routine business had been transacted, an entertainment of songs, readings, and recitations fol- lowed, in which the Chairman, Bros. Webb and Widders, Sister Lamb, and others took part. The members will be I entertained to supper on Monday next. RELIGIOUS MANIA AT WIDNES.—Cin the application of Mr. Scannell, the relieving officer, the Widnes magistrates, on Wednesday, committed Mary Ann Grant, wife of James Grunt, dock labourer, William-street, Ditton, to the asylum. She was suffering from religious mania, brought on by puerperal fever, and her conduct was at times very violent. Her cries and struggles when being taken from the cab to the police buildinzs were heartrendine. CAUGHT AT LiST.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. G. L. CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT RUNCORN.—Lnet night a meeting of the Con•ervatives of the " ,Jeetral Ward ' was held in the Public Hall. There was a large attendance of voters, amongst them being very many Liberals. Mr. W. B. Shore occupied the clatir. Mr. W. U. Verdm, the Con- servative candidate, delivered an address.—Mr. W. Rankin- son moved, and Mr. W. Whittaker seconded, a motion to support Mr. Verdin.—Other speakers followed, and ques- tions were pat. When the motion well pat it was found that there was a mafority against it, but the Chairman declared it to be carried. Cheers wete given for both candidates. WIDNES MANUFACTURERS AND THE INCREASED saissarierrr.—On Monday a special meeting of the Preecot Board of Gnarl:Bans was held at the Workhouse, Whiaon, to consider whether the Guardians should go to law with the Widnes manufacturers who are appealing aertinst the increased asseesnient. • There were ptesent.—The RbV.. I Father Finegan, Messrs. Newsome, Hall, Lowe, Griffltha, Kenwright, Leatiterbarrow, Barnacle, P. Longton, Fisher, Holm., Jackson, }Brenta, Buckley. Hall, Syder, aid S. Hartley (clerk). The subject was discussed in private, and It was eventually decided to defer consideration a week in order to see if some arrangement could not be arrived at be. tweeu the Board and the manufacturers. num) ON TEE VICAR OF FARNWORTH —The Rev. Geo. Bond, vicar of Farnworth, vrae the victim of an artful swindler last week. On We,lnesday a respectably dressed young woman, apparently the wife of a working-man, who stated she lived at Cronton, called upon Mr. Palmer, the sexton at Ran worth Parish Church, and desired him to make a grave for the burial of her son. She afterwards told a pitiful tale to the vicar, who lent her 103, and by his orders she was given a good tea in the -kitchen. On depart- ing she was also lent an umbrella to shelter her from the rain. A grave was opened in the church yard to receive the body of the deplored departed, on the following day, but neither the ,corpse has arrived or the woman been seen since her visit, and Mr. Bond has reconciled himself to the fact that he has been the dupe of an "artful dodger." Mamma* or Mess Para.—At Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, on Wednesday morning, Lieutenant Arthur Tim- mins, civil engineer, fourth son of Mr Ebenezer Timmins, of Bridgewater Foundry, was married to Miss S E Potter, s,ecoud daughter of the late Mr Jonathan ,Goddine Potter' merchant, of Raucous. Owing to the positions oc- cupied by the families of the bride and bridegroom in the town great interest was taken in the event. It had been, however, decided to conduct the ceremony as quietly am possible, and the ex ict hour net being known. there was only a select company present in the church. The bridesmaids were Miun M A Potter, sister of the bride, and Mims Ada Timtnins, sister of the bridegroom, and they and the bride were charmingly attired. Mr W B Kay officiated as best man. The bride was given away by Mr W Whittaker, and the nuptial knot was tied by the Re- W Preston, M.A. The wedding party were conveyed to and from the church in three coaches supplied by Mr 8 Yarwood, and at the conclusion of the breakfast the newly-married couple left for London. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS —On Tneelay after- noon the usual fortnightly meeting of this body was held at Dutton Werkhouse, Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton presiding. There were also present the Revs. J. v • N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, J. J. Bryant, Messrs. J. Weir, W. Handley, J. Mclntyre, J. Stokes T. Hewitt, T. Lewis, J. A. Arrowernith, J. G. Hamilton, T. Fotater, R. Ashton, E Wallington, Wm. Whittaker, E. Aaron, H. Linaker (clerk), an I W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—Mr. Handley, as chairman of the ' Finance Committee, reported that the accounts, which were passed, amounted to £1,023 4s ltd.—The chaplain of the Workhouse wrote under date the 10th of October, asking the Guardians to procure a few Bibles in order ;hat one might be presented to eac'. boy or girl en leaving school. It was at once resolved to comply with the request, on the Proposition of the Rev. J. Lockwood, seconded by Mr. Mclotyre.—An estimate of .£36 Sc, for the current half year, submitted by the School Attendance Committee, was adopted.—Mr. Aaron complained that, whereas the police ' rate of Weston amounted tq £lO5 a year, the only police- man living at Weston had been doing; duty elsewhere, and had not been on duty in Weston for above two hours a day. He did not see why they should pay £1.05 for a policeman. It was decided that the Clerk write to the Chief Constable of Chester, informing him of the complaint that had been made.

THE BANKRUPTCY ACT.-A return of the admini- stration orders in bankruptcy, under the 22nd section of the Act of 1883, made during 1884 in each County Court in England and Wales has just been issued. In the Warrington Court there were 7 applications with 95 creditors, and debts amounting to £219. Of these, seven debts were ordered to be paid in full, £23 was paid into Court, three judg- ment summonses were issued, and one commitment order was made. At Runcorn Court there was one application, 16 creditors, £4B debts, one of which was to be paid in Court: the sum of ..e2 was paid into Court. At St. Helens there was one application, nine creditors, and £4O debts, one to be paid in full ; the sum of .E 2 was paid into Court.

TERRIBLE ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN WOMAN

At Runcorn Petty Sossi,;n-e, 0-11 M.inday, John Bill, a dock labourer, who lives at 29, 13. ck Cooper-.treet, was charged with assau.t ng Jane Drury, and Also nith being drunk and disorderly. Drury had lived with the prisoner 21 years as his wife. On Saturday afternoon the prisoner went home under the influence of liquor, a thing of weekly occurrence, and a quarrel arose about tid it w.O; alleged Drury owed a worn an named Edwards. Drury ran into the street to escape his violence, but he pursued her, and, hay• log caught her, abused her with his fist, lie was taken to the police station, but as be was there Vera quiet and proinieed to behave himself, be was released. laimenately he w-nt home, knocked Drury to the floor, and gave her a blow on the eye. The eye wits in a very dreadful state, aril Dr. Mangan is of opinion that the sight of the eye wll otv-ir be properly recovereil.—Superintendent Limit said t Was stated the prisoner kicked t .e woman on the eye.—) nry said the prisoner was very good to her when sober, aud.she did not wish to . press the case.—P.S. Neild proved the drunkenness.—Mr. Brundrit said the Bench was determined to put a atop t) beating women. This assault appeared to be totally unprovoked, and the prisoner would be impri- ebbed for six weeks with bard labour. A flue of 59 and costs, es V, or seven days, was imposed for drankeriness.

div.head: MILITARY CONCERT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MILITARY CONCERT AT RUNCORN.

The second annual concert organised by the Runcorn Volunteer Band took place on Tuesday evening in the Pub- lio Hall. There was a large attendance of the public, and the concert altogether was a most successful one. The programme commenced with a capital performance by the band, of Charles Godfrey's "Nebuchadoaesor," specially written for the recent Belle Vise band contest, and Mr. James Ainsworth must be congratulated upon the skilful execu- tion displayed by those whom he directs. " The soldier's good•bye " was sung, by Mr. G. H. Taylor in a tasteful manner. accompanied on the piano by Mr. John 11 Ivens- croft. Madame Anderson achieved a great success. Her faultless style and rare tone and expression secured her a most enthusiastic recall in each of her contributions— 'When the heart is young" and "Sunshine and rain." In response she sang At eventide " and "Coning through the rye" in charming fashion. The rich volume of Miss Nellie Handley's voice, combined with her cultivatell expression, enabled her to do full justice Is Pinsuti's new song " Many a mile assay" and "Side by side to the better land," by I Hutchinson; and she won a deserved encore. She favoured ithe audience in response with "Golden love." The fact that Mr. Addison Hill was twice recalled testi- fies to the robust and tuneful interpretation he gave " I'm a roamer," and " Toe storm fiend." He raised his audience Is a high pitch of enthu- , siasm by his admirable vocalisation. The performance on I the llut3 by Mr. V. L. Neednam was a musical treat of the highest order, and be was recalled with the most hearty manifestation of pleasure. Mr. Josef Cantor was as great a fay.,urite as ever, and as vocalist and accompanist he won fresh laurels. It ought not to be forgotten that in the second part the hand played a " grand polka," in which Mr. James Woods took the solos, and excelled himself. He displayed ' a full appreciation of and control ever his instrument, and the result wee a tuneful and skilful performance. The proc-eds of the concert will be devoted to providing new brass instruments for the bi.nZ

Cartwright, solicitor, Chester, for 303 due under a judgment. Mr. A. E Day defended. His Hon- our dismissed the summons for want of evidence of RIVEDS.

A RELSBY SOLICITOR AND HIS TAILOR.-13.sers. Dug- gan Brothers and Darling, Liverpool, sued Mr. W. R. Dreaper, solicitor, Helsby and Chester, for £ll 2s Si, under A judgment summons. Mr. Day represented the defendant. His Honour said the defendant must pay the amount with costs in a month, or go to gaol 40 days. A RUNCORN SHOEDEALER SUED —The Howe Machine Company, Limited, Liverpool, claimed from John Thomas Gumbleton, Ellesmere-street, Runcorn, the sum of £9, dam- ages for breach ef agreement. Mr. Bremner, Liverpool, re- , preeented the plaintHa and Mr. F. A. Lake defended. The 1 plaintiff's case was that ' the defendant agreed to be their agent in Runcorn, and to devota his entire services to their business. A stall in the Market Hall was hired, and the de- fendant got permission to put a few samples of boots and shots on the stall, but not to stock the shop. Machines were sent down for exhibition, and a short time subse- quently the manager visited the place. He found the stall covered with boots and ahoe, and the machines were not to be seen except on going inside the shop. For the de- fence it was alleged that the defendant had consent to enter into the shoe business, and a counter clahn of £5 9s 3d commission on sales was filed to the action. His Honour said there was no dou.at that the defendant undertook to de- vote his entire services to the plaintiff. It was, however, difficult t) say what damage the company bad sustained, and he would allaw the nominal damages of £3. On the counter claim be allowed the defendant £2 5s 81. IMPORTANT POINT: AN APPEAL —A claim for £l5 for goods sold and delivered was made by Messrs T Hadfield and Company, Limited, manure manufacturers, Weston and Liverpool, against Mr A Venour, trading as Messrs Venour and Company, fire hick merchants, , Llandudno and Liverpool. The defendant had filed a counter claim for EA damages for breach of contract. Mr A Linaker ap- psared for the plaintiff, and Mr Rudd (Liverpool) for the oefendant. Defendant bad viewed a quantity of old iron at the plaintiff's works, and agreed to purchase the iron, to ha delivered to his order at Halton station. On receiving to iron the defendant objected to its quality, hence the ~ction. Mr Linaker submitted that objection should have been taken at Halton station, and Mr Rudd argued that de- 'endant could object on arrival at Edge Hill, Liverpool. div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

THE FORTHCOMING LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN.—Complete arrangements have been made for the visit of Mr. Herbert Gladstone,. M.P., to Runcorn on Tuesday next. The meeting will commence at seven o'clock. As the demand for tickets has been very great it is probable the Pub- lic Hall will be crowded long before that hour, and from six to seven a musical programme will be gone through. Mill Brow Brass Band will play selec- tions, and a song to the tune of " Wait till the clouds roll by," composed by a local gentleman for the oc- casion, will be sung. An overflow meeting will be held in Bethesda Schoolroom, and Mr. Gladstone and others will deliver addresses. At both meet- ings resolutions of welcome to the visitor of the evening, and confidence in the late Liberal admini- stration, and a declaration to use all legitimate efforts to secure the return of Mi. J. T. Brunner, the Liberal candidate for the division, will be proposed. During his stay Mr. Gladstone will be the guest of Mr. R Shaw, of the Highlands, Higher Runcorn. Mr. James Handley, J.P., president of the Runcorn Liberal Association, will occupy the chair at the chief gathering. PRIMITIVE M ETHODISM AT RUNCORN.—Tbanksgiving services for the ingatbering of the harvest took place in Greenvray-read Primitive Methodist Chapel on Sunday. The edifice had been neatly and tastefully decorated with the fruits of the earth, the general good effect Being en hanced by several skilfully wol ked and appropriate mottoes, which testified to the labours of Messrs. Joseph stubs, E. Aston, and J. Fleet. A most conspicuous object was an immense loaf weighing 66Ibs. This had been made by Mrs Billinalley. The Rev. .1. Causland, formerly of Coventry, the newly-appointed minister, preached morning and evening, and Mr. John Wilson read the lessous. There was a good congregation in the morning, and in the even- ing the building was crowded. div.p: THE HIGHWAY BYE-LAWS.

Mr. Carey reported that the deputation appointed to wait upon the officials of Gs Local Board, with reference to the ; highway bye-laws, did so about ten days ago. The archi- tect and level representatitives of the London Board were I present, arid the various points were argued one by one, and certain conclusions were arrived at. There had not been time to pat them into shape, but the whole subject would I be laid before the Board at the next meeting.

div.head: 2'RE AUDITOR'S REPORT.
div.p: 2'RE AUDITOR'S REPORT.

The Clerk read the following lettar Waterloo, Liver- pool, 3rd October,. 1885.—Gentlemen,—Io pursuance of the provisions of the Public Health Act, 1875, I bays to report that I have completed the audit of the accounts of your Board for the year ended at Lady Day last. I desire to suggest to the Board the desirability of entering into a contract or an agreement with the Medical Officer of Health specifying the remaneration to he paid that officer in respect of his Drofessioaal attendance upon persons suffering from infectious disease, and removed by the Lecal Board for the purposes of isohafion. I have grave doubts as te the legality of the expenditure Weaned by the Board in in- epectieg the highways within their district, and it was net without hesitation that I allowed the item. I trust the Board will restrict this and similar expenditure as much as Possible in the future. I think it necessary for the Board to Eire either general or specific anthorito to the surveyor and engineer to undertake journeys on behalf of the Board. I have made a report upon your accounts to the Local Government Boad, and you will be communicated with in dne course in reference thereto.—l an. gentletneu, your obedient servant, Gitonoe Hezmfuousr,Dietrict Auditor."— Toe Clerk remarked that on tbe outbreak of smallpox it was necessary that the Medical Meer should attend a case and the Board had to pay him. The auditor desired that in future fixing a fee paid should be passed. With reeard to the surveyor and engineer, all that was required was a formal resolution that these officers had authority to travel on the Board's business and charge their expenses, subject to the approval of the committee.—Mr. Carey moved, and Mr. Gaskell seconded, the formal resolution intimated. --Carried.

div.p: THE GAS COMMITTEE.

The minntes of this committee were passed, on the motion of Mr. Gaskell, seconded by Mr. Wright. The rainfall for the month was a mean of 4 335 inches, and the water in stock on the 16th ult. was 8,912. 579 valions. The water pumped during the month was 49,496,9T0 gal- lons, a decrease of 9'50 gallons on the correspondinz month last year." The gas made and delivered was 5,409,000 cubic feet, an increase of 9.42 per cent. The illuminating power of the gas was 17 c miles. The tender of Mr. J. P. Coop. St. Paul's Buildirgs, for 17 uniforms for the firemen was accepted.

HISHWAY MATTERS --THE CLOSING OF WEST BANE- . STREET.—ELIBLIC LAMPS. The Highway Committee recommended that a fence be erected around the open space in Warrington-road, and that the streets adjoining the land be laid out and cindered out of the Public Road Improvement Account at an estima- ted cost of £100; and that the tender of Mr. Tnomas Sadler be accepted. It was also recommended that a 12 inch pipe sewer he put in Market-street, along the frontage of Greenall and Company's premises, to connect with the main sewer, upon the company agreeing to pay half the cost. The Surveyor submitted a report on the traffic at Anne-street Level Crossing. The committee considered the working of the gates to be satisfactory, and that no action should he taken at present. It was recommeuded that the agreement -,vith Messrs. T. Bolton and Sons to close West Bank-st. be sealed, and that the street be made from Church- street to Marsh-st., under the provisions of the Public Health I Act. On the 24th September Mr. T. Shuttleworth, junr., wrote asking for some lamps in Wilmere-lane. The Rev. G. Bond attended respecting some at Farnworth. It was recommended ',That in future temporary bracket lamps be placed in unadopted streets for the safety of the public, and that when such streets are made under the provisions of the Public Health Act, pillar lamps be provided at the cost of property owners." It was further recommended that a lamp at SiMM'S Cross be removed to Widnes-road near to Bryon-street, and one from Little Briton to Widnes- road near to St. Paul's Church ' • that a pillar lamp be placed in Deacoo-road and in Fitt-lane—that a bracket lamp be placed at each of the following places :—Saxon terrace, Ross-street, Elliott-street, Foster-street, Elizabeth- street, and West-street—and that gas be supplied to the lamp at the old Grammar School, Farnworth. All these subject to there being gas mains already laid in the several streets, £c. It was estimated that the cost of lamps in Wil- mere-lane would be £llO, and the committee did not feel justified in recommending such an outlay.—Mr. Carey moved the confirmation of the minutes, and asked for the minute, with reference to the making of the street from Church-street to Marsh-street, be postponed. The Surveyor had another route to suggest.—Mr. Taylor seconded the motion, which Was carried. rHE NOTIFICiTION OF DISEASE. Fourteen deaths occurred amongst cl4ildren under one year, and two amongst children between one and five years. Zytnotic diseases bad caused six deaths. He had carefully examined Gerrard's Fold as instructed, and had failed to discover any nuisance. T. Whittaker had complained of a nuisance arising from a manure heap at the premises of Mr. S. Sadler. Toe Medical Officer stated there was no nuisauce injurious to health.—lt WAS recommended that medical men reporting is case or cases of infectious dis- eases (other than measles) within 24 hours of being called in, be paid a fee of 2s 61 for each such report. It was also recommended that the plans of the Infectious Diseases Hos- pital be approved, and that application be made for bor- rowing powers for £6.ooo.—The Market Inspector reported that the receipts for the market were £27 25 81, a decrease of £9 148 3ti as compared with September, 1654. The usual fair had been held and a man had been killed by falling from a swingboat. He was instructed to continue to warn owners of swingboats when on the market ground of the danger of reckless nse.—Mr. Heyes moved the confirmation of the minutes. Tnis had, however, pro- dund no result, and the committee therefore recommended that the fee be increased to 28 6d. -- THE PROPOSED INFECTIOES DISEASES 11057 ITAL. Mr. Gaskell said the recommetedation of the committee, with regard to the hospital took him by surprise. It had been stated that the hospital was not to cost at the outside more than £3,000. and that for that amount ample accom- modation would be provided. This £6,000 and the money the board was already committed to for public offices would mean the addition of 3d or 44 on the rates of the town, and they mast be prepared to pay not less than 23 64 in the L. Trade was very bad, and there were strong complaints now . that the rates were too high. He thought the atnoent pro- posed by the committee eacessive. He moved that there. commendation be referred back.—Mr. Dutton seconded with pleasure.—M. Carey undeteMod that they wocld be able to manage with one ward, but from the plans on the wall he saw that two wards were to be put up. It appeared to him that one ward HES all that was necessary.—Mr. Heyes said the committee did not ask the Board to commit themselves to this expenditure. They simply asked for powers to borrow that amount to' carry out the complete plans on the wall. It was for the. Board to say how much they would spend It the present' time.—Mr. Gaskell :If von want £3.000. borrow it. What is the use of asking for £6,000 —Mr. Husband said £6,000' was an outside figure,. to be used by the Board as they thought fit. As be understood the subject, it was intended to spend only about £1,500, and Live the remainder ready 'at band for use should an emergency arise by the outbreak of an epidemic.—Mr. Gaskell said the bills of quantities showed an expenditure of £5,730, so that there was not much of a margin.—Mr. Heves said be had net the slightest objection to the Board going hate this matter fully before borrowing powers were taken.—The Chairman said if they borrowed £6,000 on the plans put before them, they would be compelled to spend the money on carrying out those plane—Eventually, it was decided to discuss the question at a special meeting on Thursday next, and the other minutes were passed. FINANCE.—THE DISTRICT RATE. The Finance Committee recommended" that the present loan on main sewer be paid off, and that a sum not exceed- ing £25,000 be obtained on the system of equal yearly re- payments of p.incipal and interest ; and that a loan, not exceeding £8,500, for public offices be obtained on same system. Interest on both amounts 4 per cent. They fur- ther recommended with rega•d to the einking funds " that application be made to the L.G. Board for a provisional order to fix the amount of an equal annual instalment for the repayment of principal and interest in respect of moneys borrowed for water and gas purposes, and to sanction the applying such instalments to the repayment of any loans becoming due on gas and water accounts." The estimates for the six months ending March next were presented as follows :—Health, Hospital, and Market Committee estimate £553 10s 6d ; Finance £2.383 103 84 ; Highway £2,101 Sc 64: total, £5,044 as 84. It was recom- mended that a general district rate of Is in the £ be laid, estimated to produce £54002. Aecounts,amount- ing to £2,458 Os 24 were passed for payment.— Mr. Handley, in moving the adoption ef the minUtee, said that the way which the committee now recommended the loans to be taken no it woeld make a difference to the rate- pavers next year of £251. the following year £226, and so on in proportion for the next eleven years. It would in fact be a saving to the ratepayers to that extent. The rate re- commended would make 2s in the £ for the year. and, not- withstanding the remarks of Mr. Gaskell, six months ago, about the subject, tbe wink would be carried on efficiently with that rate (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Dutton seconded the motion, which was carried.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. Burgess and Chandley. ASSAULTS. Isaac Forster was summoned by Dinah Gleave, his sister, for assaulting her on the Bth inst. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant. Defendant, who lives at Bolton, came to Warrington to attend the funeral of his father, and, it was alleged, struck his sister several times, knocked her down, and then kicked her. Complain- ant only desired that be should be bound over to keep the Peace. Be was accordingly bound over in his own surety of £lO to be of good behaviour for six months. MONDAY. —Before Mr. John Fairclough and Councillor Greening. MISCELLANEOT:S.—The following persons were dealt with for drunkenness :—Thomas Farrell, in Horsemarket street, fined 5s and costs ; John Lynch, at Market Gate, dis- charged on promising to leave the town ; Ellen Connor, in Horsemarket-street. sent to prison for seven days ; Martin Melody, in Bridge•street, fined ss, including costs; John Finnegan, in Bridge-street, and Thomas Coyne, in Market- place, each tined 5s and costs; Ann Owen, in S. James- street, fined ss, including costs --Ralph Allen, charged with being a deserter from the South Staffordshire Regi- ment, stationed at Salford barracks, was remanded to Wal- ton to await escort.—William Evans was ordered to pay 2s per week towards the maintenance of his son William, on the ship "Clio."---For allowing the chimney of his house to be on fire, William Brooks was fined Is 6d, including cot.—TWO men named Tickle and Charles Cummings were charged with fighting in Mersev-street, and were ordered to find sureties for their good behaviour.—Thos. Roes, for throwing potatoes in the market was fined is, in- cluding costs. He threw a potato at another boy, who fell and was run over by the wheel of a potato cart. The boy was not, however, much injured.--Michael Welsby was fined Is and costs for wheeling a barrow on the footpath at Latchford on the 12th inst.--Two boys named Makin and Wilkinson were summoned for letting off fireworks in Mer- sey-street ; a fine of 2s each was imposed. LARCZNY.—Catherine Marr (19), fustian cutter, of no fixed abode, was sent to prison for two months, with hard labour, for stealing a skirt, a pair of clogs, and other articles, the property of Joseph Barrow, of 5, Glasshouse - square, on the previ 4US Friday. SCHOOL ArraNDANcs.—The following persons were each fined 5s for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—William Vernon, flattnan, Bank Quay; James Barker, bricksetter, Admiral-street ; James Bradshaw, Wat- kin-street • John Harper, Lilford-street. John Walker, tanner, Latchford; Robert lit:watts% Latchford ; and Henry Isherwood, warehouseman, Mersey View.—Henry Shaw, flatman, L ttchford, foto not sending his two children regu- larly to school, was fined is 6d. The cases were proved by Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett, Mr. Z. Armitage, and Dr.

Goresll. MISCELLANEOUS. - Henry Connor summoned Edvrard Green for assiuttin, him, at Latchford, on the 12th inst ; Green also summoned Connor for assaulting him on the fol- lowing day. Both were ordered to be bound over to be of good behaviour.--Mary Gandy charged her husband Ed. Gandy, with assaulting her on the 10th inst. He was ordered to find two sureties of £lO each, and be bound over himself in £2O, to keep the peace for six months' or, in de- fault, to go to prison for 14 days.--Richardßellis was summoned for assaulting his wife, Margaret BeHie, on the 21st September. The case was dismissed.—Ann Wade was summoned by Eliza Cullen for assaulting her on the 12th inst. She was ordered to find a surety of £5 to be of good behaviour, or go to prison for seven days.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS/ 'Mani:q.v.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. G. L. Davies. _

DISORDERLY CHARACTERS.—Edvrin Cook, a young man, was, on the evidence of P.C. Wallace, fined 103 and costs for using obscene language in Penketh-lane on tho 4th September. A similar penalty was imposed upon John Green for being drunk and disorderly.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY. Before Mr. J. Brock. DIEDNICHNNESS AND BEGGING.—For this offence the fol- lowing persons were fined :—Myles Rose, Peter Catterall, William Mellon, John Carroll, Thomas Lewis, Owen McCab, Patrick Lawlor, Joseph Marsh, and Matthew Gormley. John Mulroney was committed for seven days for begging.
NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS. SATIIRDIY.—Before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, W. F. Gooch, _

- A. C. McCornuodale, and C. Pilliington. DittarKENNEss.—James Handley, for being drunk and disorderly at Wargrave on the 25th September. was fined 5s and cost.—Thomas Davies was summoned for a similar offence committed at Earlestown on the 28th tilt, and was fined 5s snd costs.

CHIMNEY FIRING.—JnEeph Rice, Earlestown, was sum- moned for haying the chimney of his dwelling-house on fire on the 24th September. Mrs Rice appeared and stated that she did not knot, the chimney was on fire. She had only been in the house about three months.—The Bench inflicted a fine of 33 61, including costs.

div.head: WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART SCHOOL.
div.p: WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART SCHOOL.

The annual meeting took place in Lacey-street School- room oti Tuesday evening. The room was crowded, Mr. F. B. Gessage, J. P. chairman of the committee, presided, and there were present the Revs. J. Wright Williams, G. Bond, E. A. P. Wilson,. J. M. Jones, Father Finegan, and It. G. Hughes; Dr. Hurter, Messrs. E. Carey, It. H. Davies, R. Brawdshaw, Allan Deacon, 0. E. Smith, W. A. Watts, M.A.. J. Morrison (hon. sec.), is.c. The Rev. S. J. Perry was also present to deliver a lecture on the Government expedition to Madagascar to observe the transit of Venus, of which the rev. gentleman was the chief. The Chairman called upon the Secretary to read the 11th annual report, from which it appeared that the attendance at the classes during the past session bad been excee,iingly satisfactory. The number of individual students under in- as compared with 130 last year ; and struction WAS 147, the number of entries to cl asses was 184, as compared with 164 the previous year. 137 a udents attended the Govern- ment examinations and the results were:— No. No. Per Eamd. Passed. Cent,. Freehand drawing Machine construction lB 9 50 Building construction Mathematics 8 2 25 Inorganic Chemistry (Theoretical) 4B 13 27 do. do. (Practical) l9 10 53 Lcoustics, light. and heat The committee had decided to leave out of the syllabus mathematics and acoustics, as these classes were very badly attended last session. This would enable Mr. Watts to devote more time to chemistry, and the committee bops the alteration will result in the school regaining the high reputation hitherto held in this subject. Mr. R. H. Davis made a handsome and valuable present to the library last winter, consisting of over 100 volumes of fiction and poetry by the best authors. (Applause.) Mr. G. H. Bolton pre- sented a collection of over 40 volumes of fiction and poetry. (Applause.) The committee recorded their thanks to Mr. Davis and Mr. Bolton for their valuable gifts. Mr. H. Wade Deacon had kindly promised to lend for reference any books in his library that students or others might wish to consult. (Applause.) The committee had felt a desire to establish a lending library, hut after careful consideration concluded that with theii limited staff it could not be con- ducted sathifactorily. The committee, however, understood that in the new public offices the Local Board were erect- ing, provision would be made for a library, and when it was completed, and the ratepayors cinsented to the adoption of the Public Libraries Act, the committee would, with the donors' permission, have pleasure in placing meat of their bpoks in the hands of the Local Board, to be used for the benefit of the people of Widnes. Mr. J. L. bluspratt, chairman of the committee since the establishment of the classes in 1874, had felt obliged to resign, and the committee regretted to lose his services. Mr. F. 11. Gossage had kindly consented to accept the chalrminship. (Applause.) The balance sheet, audited by Mr. V. C. Driffield, showed that the following donations had been received :-51essrs. Gos- sage and 80118 £2O, Sullivan and Company £2O, Gaskell, Deacon and Company £2O, Muspratt and Sons £lO, Puking. ton and Son £lO, Tharsis Company £6 6s, Widnes Alkali Company £3 3., Vickers and Sons £3 3s. Mathieson and Company £3 3s, Hall Brothers and Shaw £2 2e, Golding, Davis and Company £2 2e, Hutchinson and Company La 2s, total £lO2 is D. The total receipts were £226 17s 3d, After paying all expenses there was a balance of £lO 8s 94 in the bank.

Mr. R. H. Davies then distributed the prizes to the enc.. ,cessful students In a brief address he remarked that to a Widnes audience he need scarcely say anything about the practical use of chemistry, except it was thatthey were very far behind in the rice in o.ganic chemistry. A friend study- ing under Dr. Hoff non, at Berlin, informed him that in all probibility there were not more than 20 or 30 men in Eng- land who had done good work in organic chemistry, where- as in Germany they were to be counted by hundreds. The chemical industry of Germany had derived great benefit from the high range of study in the university, lie was sorry to say that the number of students ha their science classes were not so great as they should be considering the large population of Widnes. He honed that there would be a great accession to their numbers in future. (Hear hear.) The Ray. Father Perry said that no doubt it was true chemistry WAS studied in a great part in Germany, but if they wanted to study astronomy stay in England. There was net in the whole world astronomers equal to the gentle- men of England. (Applause.) Having referred to the utility of astronomy, he proceeded with his lecture, which was illustrated by diwzrams and photographs, thrown on a screen by the lime light. He described graphically the expedition to. Desolation Island in 1874 to view the transit of Venus. On the motion of Mr. Carey. seconded by Mr. A. Deacon, a vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, and a similar compliment having been paid the chairman on the motion of Dr. Hurter, seconded be Mr. Morrison, the meeting con- cluded.

CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT DOWEALL GREEN. 03 Monday evening, a Conservative meeting was held in the Rectory Schools, Downall Green, to hear a lecture nn " Political Topics," by Mr. F. W. Deacon. There was a good attendance. Mr. C. F. Clark presided. Resolutions were passed in support of the Government and et the can- didature O ir Richard Cross,

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

Foomau...—Gotborne Association v. Liverpool Post Office. —Cup Tie.--Lovers of football had a rare treat provided them on the Recreation Ground, Golborne, last Saturday, when the home club tried conclusions with the Liverpool Post Office representatives. The event was the first round of the Liverpool and District Cup competition,' and a capi- tal game it proved. Golborne winning with flying colours. The game ended in favour of Golborne by five to nil. The Edge Green Brass Band was in attendance and discoursed lively airs. F. R. Jones, the Welsh international man, Played splendidly, and but for his efforts many more goals would doubtless have been scored. FLOWER Snow.—Mr. and Mrs. Nichols, of the Leigh Arms Rotel, Golborne, inaugurated a flower show last Sat- urday on a large scale. The exhibits were staged in the large public diniug-room upstairs, which was elegantly de- corated for the occasion. Upwards of a hundred prizes, in- cluding Silver teapots and other valuable articles were offered, and competition was keen in most of the Classes. The vegetables were exceptionally good, and the fruit and flowers were of the finest order. The show was numerously attended during Saturday and Sunday. The judging was in the hands of M-. Randall and Mr. Wilson (Newton-le- Willows), and Mr. Bell, florist, of Wigan.

Louis Riel, who was to have been hanged on Friday, has been further respited until the .16th inst. Her Majesty's gunboat Dwarf ran on the rooks at Holyhead on Monday night. She is believed to be much injured. The Heywood magistrates on Saturday committed for trial an old man named John Ryder, who had obtained from a wine and spirit dealer several bottles of whiskey and pot on the false representation that his wife was dead and he wished to " Wake" her.

div.head: GENERA.L NEWS.
div.p: GENERA.L NEWS.

The Salvation Army barracks at New Wortley, Leed. were burned down on Tuesday. Robert Wilson was tined £4O, at Glasgow, for having sold methylated spirits as a beverage, Miss Catherine Thompson, Penrith, who died a few days ago' has b-queathed £l,OOO t ) the Salvation Army. Sir Charles Warren has accepted an invitation to dinner to be given in his honour by the London Chamber of Com- merce on the 21st inst. A young man named Tucker and his sweetheart, Jane Harvey, were drowned through the upsetting of a pleasure boat at Exeter on Sunday. George Potter, a pensioner, returning to Clonmel on Thursday night, was beaten and thrown into the river Suir. Potter saved himself from drowning.. . .

A fire broke out on Thusday evening in the lace factory of Messrs. Jacoby and Co., Broadway, Nottingham, and damage was done to the amount of £20,00. A. Central News telegram, dated St. Petersburg, Thus. day, states :—Sara Becker, the Socialist, charged with an atrocious murder, has been acquitted by the jury after a trial lasting ten days. Mr. Gladstone has promised to give £lO towards the , university extention scheme in Northumberland, to be pre- sented to the most successful student on the same conditions as the prize given by Miss Gladstone last year. The Broad Arrato says it is in ‘‘ a position to announce that the Government have it in contemplation to annex the whole of Burmah," and that they had been ;advised to descend upon King Theebanos capital with 10,00 Indian troops. A Great Eastern train from London, on arriving at Hard- wick Bridge, King's Lynn, on Monday morning, dashed into a flock of sheep. which stayed on the line, killing ' between 40 and 50. The engine and carriages kept on the rails. _ _ _

_ THE TRADE COMMISSION.—The Royal Commission upon trade held another meetiag in London on Thursday. Lord Iddesleigh was in the chair, and most of the commissioners were present Mr. Taylor, of the Bankruptcy Department. was the first to give evidence, and other witnesses fol- lowed. . . .

THE MUNSTER BAN.—Preparations are beine made to re-open on Monday next the Munster Bank, Dublin, as the Munster and Leinster Bank. with the haads of the old establishment, while the provisional liqui- dators will continue realising the asbeta of the defunct concern. .

_ MURDEROUS ATTACK AT ROCHDALE.-At half-put one on Tuesday morning P.C. Rose found John Kelly, Roch- dale, bleeding from wounds on his head. Kelly stated that at bait-past ten the previous night he was seized by three men, and thrown over the rails from the footpath into the road beneath, a distance of about 1511. He is in a danger- ous state. .

TERRIBLE ArTBMPT AT MURDER.-At Manchester, on Tuesday. Lawrence Flynn was committed to the assizes charged with attempting to murder Kate Hines. The pri- soner, when apprehended, said "I intended to murder her; I took a piece of iron under my coat, and went to meet her as ahe was coming out of the workhouse." With the iron he struck her several times heavily on the head.

Gaudnrr RESCDE.—A brave rescue was affected by Thomas White, coastguardsman, near Sunderland, on Sun- day night. Six children, who were missing, were believed to be in a cave under the cliffs, and, owing to the height, dangerous to get at. White was lowered from the top, and found the children almost senseless and waist deep in water, the tide being high. Five were brought to the top, and the other had to be carried through the water. lap OLDHAM STRIKE —The Mayor of Oldham has offered his services to act as arbitrator, with a view to bring the strike te an end. The Mayor suggests aa uncon- ditional 71 per cent reduction. The proposal has creatPd much excitement in the borough.and is favourably received. Amongst the operatives, however, dissatisfaction is ex- pressed that his worship should have suggested 71- per Cent las a compromise. It is said that the Clarence Mill, Chad- derton, will open on Monday en the operatives' terms. BRUTAL MIMI/HR.—On Monday, two men named Hill , and Williams, were committed for trial on the cliarge of wil- fully murdering a female hop-picker. The prisoners, on ' the night of September 13th, followed deceased and another 1 woman across the fields, and attempted to improperly as- sault them. The women resisted, and one of them escapod, , but the other continued to strugee, with the result , that the prisoners lost their tempers, and beat the unfor- tunate woman about the bead with heavy sticks until life 1 was extinct.

THE TRADE COMMISSION.—The Glasgow Chamber of Commerce, replying to a circular from the Royal Commis- sion on Trade, say that they have no answer so precise or reliable as to adequately convey to the Commissioners the information they desire. Tne Chamber states, however, that the workmen in Glasgow, except those employed in shipbuilding yards, are getiorally well employed, with good wages, which have a purchasing power never before known. Certain of the directors think the Factory Acts should be re- vised to meet foreign competition. ACCIDENT TO THH DUCHESS OF EDINBURGII.—kn ex- press train, by which the Duchess of Edinburgh, with the Countess Erbach-Battenberg, was returning from HeiWel- , berg, met with an accident on Sunday near Darmstadt by collision with the rear of a goods train. None of the pas- sengers suffered injury, although several luggage wag- gone were wrecked. The Duke of Edinburgh received the Duchess at Darmstadt, intending to proceed to Cologne with her, but in consequence of the accident they re- mained for the night at the Grand Ducal Castle, and left on Monday night.
