I thought I wou'd get one of your • Willonia' Betts, and am glad to say that I found much good retult therefrom; so much so that I am considerably st onger. and I am now able to fodow my regular work and can with confidence recommend your Belts ta all who suffer as I did.—Yours faithfully, WM. THOMPSON, 52, Granville street, Balford."—The Wilsonia " also cures Lumbago, Indigestion, Asthma. Paralysis, Loss of Vital and Nerve Power; General Debility. &c.—Can only to obtained of WM. Wasow, Medical Electrician, Exchange A, cads, Man- chester .—./Idrt. SALES FOR EXTRAORDINARY TITHES.-00 Saturday, at the instance of the Vicar of Ticeihurst, Sussex, two separ- ate sales for extraordinary tithes on hop gardens belonging to old parishioners and Churchmen, and amounting to- gether to about £6O, were effected by an auctioneer from Berkshire. An indignation meeting followed, presided over by Mr. Bolton, president of the Anti-Extraordinary Tithe Association, and a resolution was passed expressing the win. ion that the tithe was an impediment to agriculture, and should, therefore, be abolished, and hoping that a reformed Parliament would remove from the statute book the law authorising the tithe. DISPSTABWInigNT.—The agitation for the disestiblish- ment of the Church of England was the subject of discus- sion at the Eccles rari-decanal half-yearly meeting on Sat- urday, and a resolution was passed appointing a committee to provide funds for Church defence. The subject was in- troduced at a meeting of the Hulme Ruri-decanal Sunday School Union on Saturday, when a member moved a resolu- tion affirming that it was the paramount duty of every Churchman to use every means in his power to prevent Mr. Agnew, a supporter of Disestablishment, being returned at the next election. Another member objecting that notice ought to have been given of the motion, the Caairman con- curred, and the subject dropped. TERRIBLE POACHING AFFRAY IN NORTH WALES. , —A serious poaching affray was investigated by the Den- bigh magistrates on Saturday. Ten poachers. including, it was stated, T and D. Davies, sow before the Bench, invaded at night the Dyffryn Aled estate. They were pounced upon by Constable Davies. A. Smith, head keeper, R. Williams, under keeper, and J. Kelly, footman. A murderous fight ensued. The constable was knocked down and kicked till he became insensible. Smith seized one man, and locked in each others arm they fell into a river, and he also lost con- sciousness. Williams had three teeth kicked clean out of his mouth, and was also dreadfully cut. He rescued hie comrade from the river. All the.poachere got clear away, leaving the keepers in a shocking state. The two prisoners were remanded. Lusa NATIONAL LEAGLIE.—A meeting of the St. Helens branch of this league was held in the Public Hall, liardshaw-street, on Monday evening. It had been an- nounced that Mr. Cox. of Warrington, would give a lecture on "The duty of Irishmen at the corning election," but this gentleman was unable to be present, and Mr. Michael Con- way, of Blackburn, attended. Mr. Doran, vice-president, opened the proceedings, after which Dr. Donnellan (presi- dent) took the chair. There was a large attendance. Mr. John Denvir, district organiser, delivered an address, and dwelt upon the necessity for the Irishmen of St. Helens holding aloof from all political parties. Mr. Michael Con- way also dwelt on the importance of Irishmen refusing to pledsze themselves to any party until Mr. Parnell and the I Irish parliamentary party had decided on which side the Irish vote could be cast to best serve the Irish cause.—Mr. Enright nroposed a hearty vote of [banks to Mr. Conway and Mr. Denvir for their addresses.—Mr. Doran seconded the motion, which was carried and responded to A vote of thanks having been accorded to the Chairman, the proceed- ings terminated. WORKMEN'S TRIBUTE TO MR GrAnszoten.—On Monday night a meeting of the executive committee of this move- ment was held at the City Liberal Club. Walbrook. There was a numerous attendance.—Mr. F. A. Ford, the chairman of the committee, congratulated the meeting on the result of their first week's work. Delegates had already been ap- pointed from many democratic political institutions, as well as from trade, temperance, and friendly societies. Sir John Lubbock, M.P., had consented to act as joint treasurer with Mrs. Fenwick Mil Irr and Mr. A. Callow. With reference to the "Gladstone Tribute Stamp," application for the gift of a design had been made to Sir John Millsis,R.A., and at the next meeting it eas hoped the committee would he in pos- session of a design of artistic merit and intrinsic worth. Happily the tri,‘ute work assisted rather than retarded e'en-

• . . 1 ..............._ ....._..... ..........____ _ tioneering, because it bitcaine more apparent every day that the name of Mr. Gladstone would be the cry to control the constitteencies —Mrs. Feriwick Miller remarked that the great object of the promoters of the movement was to show to Mr. Gladstone while he lived some tangible token of the people's appreciation end gratitude—Various suggestions were made with the view of securincr the co-operation of the working classes in the provincial' centres of England and Scotland, and the lion. secretary, Mr. Rann, was in- ' structed to open communication with that object in all the great towns. .
KAY'S COMPOUND, for Colds and floughq. Sold throughout the World, 9,d, Is lid, 2s 9d, &e. Kay, Brothers, Stockport. —Advt.
E ARLESTOWN.

EsardisrowN Foornam. Cum.—A general meeting of the members of this club was held at the Conservative Club, Earle-street, on Tuesday evening, to take into consideration rules for the management of the club which had been drawn up and adopted lay the committee. There was a large at- tendance of members, and Mr. P. Hastie presided. The rules, which numbered 19, were read and fully considered, and a motion was unanimously passed that they be adopted and printed.

DI-TURBANCE AT TEM MARKET.—Margaret Jones, a marlied woman' hailing from Warrington, was charged at the Town Hall, Newton. on Saturday, with being drunk and disorderly on ths Market Place, Earlestown, on the previous evening.—P.C.'s Hunt and Lee stated that about eleven o'clock on the previous nighL they heard a disturbance on the MatkA. On going thither they found the prisoner drunk, cursing and swearing in the midst of a crowd of people.—She was fined 58 and cost. _

SiPaux.r. TO A.FIGHT.—Ar the Newton Patty Sessions, on Saterday, Henry Davies and James Dowd, young men, were summoned for committieg a breach of the peace by fighting at Earlestown on the 4th inst.—Dowd pleaded guilty, adding that he was in drink at the time, and he Was sorry. The other defendant said he was not guiltv.—P.C. Lloyd spoke to seeing the defendants fighting in Earle- street, with their coats off, and in the midst of a great crowd. On seeing him they ran into the Griffin Hotel.— P.C. Hunt gave similar evi Icons, and the defendants were bound over to keep the peace for six months. SIIOCKINO CRUELTY TO Cows—Before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, W. F. Gooch, A. C. McCorquodale, and C. Pilk- ington, at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Thomas ; Rafferty, an Irish cattle dealer, was summoned for cruelty to two oows at Newton Fair, on the 11th August.—lnspec- tor Nicholls, of the Boval Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Anirnala,prosecnted, and stated that the defen- dant was in charge of a number of cows at Newton Fair. Two of them were very much overstocked with milk, and as a conseqaence the animals suffered very great pain. The udders were swollen to the utmost sxtent, and were very much inflamed. He spoke to the defendant about their condition, and he said he had kept them uninilked for a longer period than usual owing to the bad market. In reply to the Bsnch the Inspector said the dealers kept the cows unmilked in order to make buyers believe that they were better milkers than they really were.—The defendant did not appsar, and the Bench inflicted a fine of 40s and costs.

BAPTIST SUNDAY SeHoor..—The quarterly meeting of the teachers connected with the Baptist Sunday school, Market-street, Earlestown, was held on Wednesday. There was a full attendance, and after the company had partaken of a subtantial tea, Mr. G. F. Aveline (superintendent) oc- cupied the chair. Mr. B. Harrison was appointed joint superintendent with Mr. Aveline, the latter gentleman be- ing in charge of the senior classes in addition to his duties as superintendent. During the evening the chairman in- timated that there was an increased number of scholars in the senior classes, and the general conduct of the scholars throughout the school was g )od. Mr. D. Bains-Griffiths at- tended the meeting and urged the formation of a branch of the Band of Kindness, such as was in existence at the Wes- leyan school. He explained that its objects were to incul- cate into the minds of children habits of kindness to all God's creatures. The teachers promised to give the matter their careful consideration.

RAILWAY AOCIDENT AT ELI:MYST° W N F Shortly after seven o'clock on Monday night an accident occurred at Earlestown Station, by which the passenger traffic was delaye4 and one of the lines blocked for a con• eiderable time. An engine belonging to the passenger train due to start for Wigan a: 7-35 had been shunting a train of empty coaches into a siding near the Warrington Junc- tion signal box, and was returning to the main line when the wheels of the tender struck the points, throwing the tender off the line. A telegram for assistance was at once despatched to Warrington, and on the arrival of a break- down gang with proper appliances about nine o'clock the engine was soon placed upon the rails, and the line was cleared. In the meantime another engine had been obtained, and the train for Wigan proceeded on its way about half an hour late. Fortunately no trains were due along the line blocked by the engine off the rails for two hours after the accident occurred, otherwise great inconvenience would have been occasioned.

FURTHER SHORT TINE AT THE VULCAN. The slack- ness of trade and the absence of orders at the Vulcan iron- foundry is being more severely felt than was anticipated a week ago. We then stated that the men were being stopped on Saturdays, but a further adoption of short time is announced. On Wednesday a notice was posted on the board in the card of the foundry stating that on and after Monday next the whole of the hands, numbering some hun- dreds, will only be employed each day from nine o'clock in the morning until half-pasr five at night. The works will be closed entirely on Saturdays. The serious nature of this notice will be evident when it is stated that up to lately the workmen commenced at nine o'clock on Mondays only, while on the morning of each other day, including Saturday, they started at six o'clock. On Mondays' Tuesdays, and Wednesdays they were stopped at 5.30, en Thursdays and Fridays at six o'clock, while on Saturdays they worked until twelve o'clock. The notice virtually means that the workmen will only be found work for four full days in each week.

VACCINATION SITSCHONSES.— Al the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, W. F. Gooch, A. C. McGorquodale, and C. Piluington, John Mus- croft, residing in Nelson-street, Earlestown, was summoned for failing to have his ohild vaccinated.--The defendant pleaded guilty, and said he thought he had a strong reasen for doing so. The first child he had vaccinated was the first child he had born, and it was healthy and strong until it was vaccinated, but it had to be buried a month later.— The Chairman (Mr. Gillespie) : Do you intend to have the child vaccinated ?—Defendant replied that he did pot. He I strongly objected for the reason he had stated. He was sure if any one had seen the suffering of his child they would' never have had another of their children vaccinated. He had to stay up night and day with it, and it had to be buried month after it was vaccinated.—The Chairman: We have pnly to administer the law, and you will be fined 58 and oests.—There was a further summons against the defendant for a similar offence, and also against James Woods, clogger sad bootruaker, Queen-street, and James Ashcroft, Crow- lane.—The Clerk (Mr. White) it : These are cases for vaccination orders which must be heard by the same magis- trate who signed the summons. Mr. Houghton is not here, and therefore the summonses must be either dial:rib/led, Or ,Tijourned,—Tbe Bench said they would be adjourned until the next 6(.1551005. A rhUrt BilkintrETa WESLEYAN CnaPEL.—A very pleasant gathering, and one new to the district, was held in the Lectare Hall beneath the Brunswick Wesleyan Chapel, Cross-lane, Rarlestown, on Monday evening. It was announced as a "Fruit Banquet "—the proceeds of which were in aid of the fund being raised for the purchase of an organ for the chapel—and it was certainly one of the most enjoyable gatherings held in connection with that place of worship for a considerable time past. A large number of persons attended. The tables, well stocked with grapes, apples, plums, and other fruit, were still farther en- hanced in beauty by choice flowers and plants, kindly placed at the dißposainf those having charge of the arrange- ments br Mrs. J. W. Emmett. For the entertainment of. the visitors a short hut excellent programme had been drawn up. The 'resident minister, the Rev. James Kent, opened the proceedings with an appropriate address on the pi'easant character of such gatherings. , During the evening Mr. Peter Hasa% whose abilities ever make him_ popular with an Earlestown. audience, sang

"Over the Rolling Sea" and "The Man of War." ife ware enthusiastically recalled on each occasion, and he gave as encores "The Little Hero" and "Polly." Miss Hulse and Miss Needham sang the duet "Let music and song be our pastime to-day," Master and Miss Stringer gave the piano- forte duet "le banks and braes," Mr. Mee sang "Consider the lilies," and Mr. Burgess gave two excellent re angs. Miss E. L. Greerall, the accomplished organist of the chapel, presided at the pianoforte, and to her efforts much of the success of the gathering is clue. During an interval the fruit was handed round to the company by a band of girls. The pryceedings last.d about two hours, ana con- cluded with thanks to friends who had contributed to its success.

A SINGULAR CASE.—John Houghton, of Newton, was charged at the Newton Petry Sessions, on Saturday, to show cause why he should not be committed to gaol for the non- payment of arrears under a bastardy order obtained by Ann Southern. It was stated that the arrears amounted to al. Bs., and the case had been adjourned to give the defendant an opportunity of making some arrangement with the com- plainant. The latter now stated that the defendant had not done anything since the adjournment—Defendant : I have done nothing only try to agree with her and she won't have it.—The Clerk: Are you p-epared Vs pay the £ll 10s? Defendant: No; I have been playing over 12 months. —He handed tap a medical certificate stating that he was suffering front lumbago and debility and was unable to fol- low any employment—The Clerk said he brought a similar certificate at the last hearing, but he was told to bring the doctor himself.—The Chairman: Is your wife in a good position to assist you with regard to the furniture 7—De- fendant : We have very little furniture —Mrs. Houghton (defendant's wife) then stepped forward and she was in- termed by the Bench that if her husband did not pay the arrears he could be sent to prison.—Mrs. Houghton : E have four little children and I have to work very hard to keep them.—The Chairman: Are you prepared to offer this woman (complainant) anything P—Mrs. Houghton : No, sir.—Deferalant : I cm offer her 103. That is all the means I have. I told her on Wednesday I would pay her when I got work—Complainant: He wants to get cut of it during the next two years arid then he thinks his debt NCR be wiped off.—ln reply to the Clerk, defendant said he was in prison some years ago for not paying to the order.-1 he Chairman (to the complainant): Would you rather take lOs now and accept his word t lat he will make regular pay- ments, or run the chance of losing the money if he goes to prison I—Complainant : If he would make come arrange ment about starting to pay I would:not mind taking the 10s- -Defendant's wile: We will pay 10s. per month.—The

Clerk : That is merely continuing the order, and it is pay- ing nothinz for the arrears.—ln reply to the Clerk, the complair,ant said she was now a married woman.—The Chairman (to &fendant): We have no alternative/ but to send you to pf icon for two months, .£100,000,000 in the COURT OF CHANCERY!—Cos A; Co., 41, Southampton-buildings, Holborn, London, W. 0., have just published a het of the heirs to this wealth. Reader, send a postal order for Is ed, and they will forward you this valu- able list, and if you find by It that you are entitled to any , money or property claim your own. Cox & Co. will show you ' the way.—Advt.

DRAGOON GUARDS AT NEWTON.—On Saturday after. noon, about half-past ten, a troop of the sth Dragoon Guards, ea route from Edinburgh to Aldershot, passed through Newton. There were about 65 horses and men, and their passage through the town excited some interest. They were billeted from Saturday to Monday at Warring- ton.

CONSERVATIVE OMB BILLIARD HANDICAP.—During the present week a billiard handicap for valuable prizes, kindly presented by Mr. T. J. Gillespie. JP., of Newton, has been commenced at the Conservative Club. The first is value .£2 10s. second £1 10s, third and fourth 108 each. The games are 100 points. The interest in the competition is evidenced by the large number of entries, no fewer than 86 members having been handicapped. THE HOPE 31,' EARLESTOWN Lodge of Good Tern- plars held its weekly session on Monday night, when Bro. George Clarke, W.C.T., presided. The principal business was the completing of arrangements for the annual tea party, and in accordance with the programme "Roll call and special visitation " the list of members was read over. It WAS decided that the absentees should be visited and re- ports thereon given at the next session. COLONEL MCCORQUODALE'S CANDIDATURE.—We under- stand that Colonel George McCorquodale the Liberal can- didate' far the Newton division of South-west Lancashire, has appointed Mr. F. Broadbridge. solicitor, Harrington-street, Liverpool, as his election agent during the forthcoming contest, in accordance with the requirements of the Act of Parliament. Colonel McCorquodale is, we believe, about to address a series of meetings throughout the division. THE UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE.—A. party of 40 temperance workers left Earlestown on Tuesday morning to attend the annual breakfast, council, and public demonstra- tion at Manchester, under the auspices of the United King- dom Alliance. They journeyed by the 6-45 a.m. train, and after spending a pleasant day in Manchester, and thoroughly enjoying the unanimity and enthusiasm which was shown amongst the temperance community gathered together, they left for home at 10-50 p.m. SOCIAL GATHERING. The members and a few friends of the Eariestown Anti-Compulsory Vaccination Society partook of an excellent tea in the Good Templars' Lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Saturday evening. About 60 persons were present, and Mc: John Clarke (president) occu- pied the chair. The proceedings were of a social character, addresses by the Chairman and Messrs. ..f. Pearson, B. Har- rison, and W. Gilmour being pleasantly interspersed with songs by Mr. Woffinden and a reading, entitled " Sailing for bacon." by Mr. George Clarke. A vote of thanks was heartily accorded to the ladies who presided at the tables, and the chairman.

A GLASS arm CHINA. Sans—One of the most supe- rior and extensive stocks of Porcelain, Dresden, and Balopian china, earthenware, and other fancy goods gathered together in Earlestown for some years was on Wednesday brought together in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown. They were a consignment of breakfast, dinner, and tea ser- vices, ornamental figures, groups, drc , sent down by manu- facturers for sale by auction, and the services of Mr Edward Edwardson, auctioneer, Earlestown, were engaged. The sale commenced on Wednesday night, and was again held on Thursday afternoon and evening. It will be again com- menced at the same hours te-day (Friday), and we would commend it to the notice of those parties who desire to secure really first-class articles at a low price.

SUCCESS OF NEWTON GREYHOUNDS.—The Ricbzway Club Coursing Meeting was commenced on Wednesday. In the North Lancashire Stakes for 166 dog puppies, first round, Mr. T. Stone's (Newton-le-Willows) Scorcher defeated Mr. Hornby's Itiero, while Mr. Stone's Soeneshifter was beaten by Mr. Hornby's Hospodar. In the second round Scorcher threw out Mr. Houlker's Hope of Revidge. On Thursday, Scorcher ran in splendid style and defeated Mr. Fletchet's Flete in the third round. The stakes were divided by Messrs. Stone, R. Jardine,and W. Anstruther. In the first round for the Clifton cup, for all aged dogs, at Di 103 each, with a piece of plate value £5O, Mr. Stone's Skittles beat Mr. Puking. ton's Petrarch, and in the succeeding rounds Skittles de- feated Mr. Lea's Lara, and Sir W. Anstruther's Altcar. The final between Skittles and Sir T. Brocklebank's Bay Tree was run yesterday (Friday.) In the Peel stakes for 12 pup- pies, Mr. Stone's Swagger Was thrown out by Mr. Pilking- ton's Peccavi, while Mr. Stone's Sensational defeated Mr. Buckley's Bold Eye, and in the next round defeated Mr. Svvinburne's Sanyasi. The final was run on Friday.

ALLEGED COERCION AT THE VIADUCT WORKS. A letter having appeared in a Liverpool Conservative newspaper respecting what the correspondent ( " A looker- on ") termed the Radical screw at E arlestown." Mr. D. Williams, of Earle-street, Earlestown, has written denying the false statements made therein. Mr. Williams adds : " As a workman I positively deny the accuracy of such ea statement, and be it understood that there is no connection between me and either of the political organisations ; and, in addition, my 15 years' official, life in connection with trade unions in this district (which embraces South-west Lanca- shire) coupled with being secretary to the local branch fot 10 years, such a position constitutes me as a kind of receptacle for all kinds of com- plaints, but never have I heard any expressions indicating any such treatment from any person or party. My fellow workmen have at times seemed curious to know what side our chief officials tcok as they appeared to be 80 indifferent, and the position of the other officials within the works stand at about seven Conservatives and twelve Liberals." "A Conservative Eanployo" also writes to the same effect. He says that he had been in the ser- vice of the cernpany at Earlestown for 15 years, and al- thongh he was both a Conservative and a Churchman, he never had nor ever heard of the " screw " being applied at any times in matters either religious or political. Such matters have always been shut out of the works gates. The letter from " A Looker On " excited some dissatis- faction amongst the workmen employed at the Viaduct, Works, and a mass meeting of the workmen was called on Thursday night, at half-past five, outside the works, to pro- test against such an accusation. A workman presided, and nearly the whole of the employes (Liberals and Con- servatives) were present. The following resolution was unanimously adopted :—" That we, employes of the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company's waggon works at Earlestown, in mass meeting, take this the first oppor- tunity of contradicting the untruthful and grossly false statements made by "A Looker On, in a letter under the heading of 'Radicalism at the Earlestown Railway Works,' published in the Liverpool Courier of tha 14th inst."

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY. OCTOBER 17, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY. OCTOBER 17, 1885.
THE NEW CENIETERY.-CONSECRATION BY THE
BISHOP.

The Church of &gland portion of the cemetery pro- vided for the township of Newton was consecratcd by the Bishop of Liverpool, on Wednesday afternoon. The want uf a public burial ground had long been forced anon the attention of the Newton Improvement Commissioners, and the rapidly increasing scarcity of burial accommodation in the various church yards compelled them to move in the matter of providing a new cemetery for the district. Afier considerable deliberation they fixed upon a -plot of land in Park-road—leading from Newton to Wargrave—se the most suitable site for the cemetery, and ultimately adopted it. The selection, however, at first caused some'dissatisfaction to a portion of the Earlestown ratepayers, and it was strongly condemned at a public meeting which was held. The, Commissioners, however, met with several insur- mountable difficulties in the way of securing a suitable site elsewhere, and their original selection was up-held Since then the site would appear to bays given satisfaction to all parties, and the cemetery which has been provided is beau- tifully laid out and extensive, and it is certainly a credit and an ornament to the township. The land measures Si acres and was purchased at a cost of £350 from the agent to Mr. W. J. Legh, M.P. It has been surrounded by a stone wall with railings, and is approached from the Park-road by a handsome carriage drive pleasantly planted with trees and shrubs. The ground has been apportioned to the various denominations as follows: Church of England,,3 acres; Nonconformist, 4- acres, Roman Catholics, acre;' and un- appropriated, 1 acres. The remainder is taken up with car- riage drives, Chapel, and cemetery-keeper's house. It may be stated that both the Congregational and Roman Catholic denominations have private burial grounds attached to their places of worship, which, it is expected, will meet their re- quirements for some years to come. Numerous trees and shrubs have been planted about the 'grounds, and give it a very pleasing appearance. A brick chapel has been provi- ded for the use of all denominations, and this—a suitable and attractive-looking building—has been erected in the centre of the cemetery. The cemetery-keeper's house stands at the entrance to the ground, where the carriage drive from Park-road ends. It is at present occup ,d by Mr. John Kettle who has been appointed to the post. The total ex- pense, including the cost of the land, was nearly £5,000. The plans and specifications were prepared by Mr. Richard Briefly, clerk and surveyor to the Newton Improvement Commissioners, under whose directions the ground was laid , out and the planting with trees, shrubs, &c. carried out. The contract for the erection of chapel, lode, was-se- cured by Mr. John Rothwell, St. Helens; the rood miking, eite„, was done by Mr. Cunlifio, of Legh, and the trees and shrubs were supplied by Messrs. Thomas Stead and Sort, Bold, Richard Boardman, and George Hilton, junior, Newton.

The ceremony of consecrating the Church of England portion took place at three o'clock in the afternoon, when among thaw) present were Mr. T. J. Gillespie, JP., Mr. B. B. Glover Mr. Thomas Hunt, Mr. George Ratcliffe (Com- missioners), Mr. James E. Woreley (law clerk), Mr. R. Brierley (surveyor), Rev. T. R. Matthews and Rev. Lovett (vicar and curate of St. John's Church, Harlestown), Rer. Mr. Pugh (curate of St. Peter's Church, Newton). Rev. C. Ward, Newton Grammar School; Messrs. C. H. F. Bor. ron, lA:reboil, James Davies, Beesley (architect), and others. The Bishop awl clergy robed themselves in the lodge at the entrailce gates. On leaving the lodge they were met by the gentlemen named, and Mr. T. J. Gillespie presented to the Bishop the petition of the Commissioners, requesting his Lordship to consecrate that portion of the ground set apart for the burial of the dead according to N rites of the Church of England ,The Bishop then called upon his secretary (Mr. Farmer) to read the petition, and this having been done, his Lordship said he would be happy to accede to the prayer of the petition. A procession was then formed in the following order :—The Bishop's Secre- tory (Mr. Farmer), the Bishop, the Rev. T. R. Matthews and Rev. G. Lovett, Rev. Mr. Pugh and Rev. C. Ward, Mr.'l Gillespie, Mr. B. B. Glover, Mr. J. E. Worslev and Mr: R. Brierlev, Mr. T. Runt and Mr. G. Ratcliffe, Messrs. Birchall, doughton, and Frost. They walked round the Church of England portion of the cemetery, the clergy audibly repeating certain portions of scripture. Ou arriving back at therlodge the Bishop directed his sec. eatatv to read the deed of consecration. His Lordship then

proceeded with the consecration service, and afterwards gave a brief address. They were aware, he said, that there was some novelty in the proceedings of that day. He had been ready and willing to consecrate a portion of the ceme- tery, and he had no hesitation in doing so though a separ- ate chapel for the service of the Church of England clergy had not been provided. That made no difference to him, for the clergy of the district could use their own dis- cretion as to what they would do—whetker or not they did as the clergy in Scotland—have the service conducted from the church to wlticia the deceased belonged. It was quite possible to do that, but he would leave it to their discretion Cemeteries were set apart as the long home of the people— and all were sure to come sooner or later and surely an occasion like that brought solemn thoughts to their minds. In ancient times the people reverenced the dead, and Egyptian mummies and 1 mausoleums showed they thought man should not be buried as a dog, but as possessing reason and intelligence, and that his body ought to be treated with respect. Then how much more should Christians regard the dead with respect. He I trusted their cemeteries would impre.s useful and lasting lessons upon them, and said he did not think they should be gloomy wretched places. He thought the funerals in this land were too gloomy, and unbecoming to them as Christians looking forward to a resurrection. He concluded by hoping that cemetery would become the scene of many earnest thoughts, many fervent prayers, many good resolu- tions, and many determinations as men turned away from the graves of those they loved, and cause them to break off from past sins, to live holy and Godly lives, and think more of the world to come. Ile proceedings then concluded with the Benediction.

THE EARLESTOWN ANTI-VACCINATORS, PUBLIC MEETING. Under the auspices of the Earlestown and District Anti- compulsory Vaccination Society a public meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Tuesday evening. There was a crowded attendance, and the proceedings were very enthusiastic. Mr. John Clarke (president) presided, and he wan supported by Dr. Robinson, of Dukenfield, Dr. Brown, of Rochdale, Mr. B. Harrison (Earlestown), Mr. J. Pearson (Earlestown ) The Chairman said they had been labouring for many years to get the obnoxious Vaccination Acts repealed, and he was glad to say that their labours had not been in vain. Ten or twelve years ago things were much different to what they wire to-day. At the outset of the prosecutions the magistrates could think of nothing less than 208 and costs, but what was their idea be (the chairman) could not say. It had been said and thought that if they inflicted fines of 203 and costs there would be no more heard of the anti- vaccinators. Mr. Sutten made some remarke of that sort, but some little time later he found that instead of ex- tinguishing the anti-vaccinators there was an addition to their number, and the fined were not now 20s and costs, but a great deal less. In the midst of all the prosecutions—he might say persecution they had had to endure he thought not one belonging to their society had wavered, but they seemed to be as determined as ever te stand to the test. Some might say that they had been too hard on the can- didates for Parliamentary honours, but many of them would know why the anti-vaccinators were so determined. About eight years ago there was a discussion in Parliament on the question, but the compulsory clauses were not yet repealed, and if they allowed those gentlemen to go to Parliament without questioning them and bringing them to the test it might be another seven years would pass over before they bad the laws erased from the statute book. That was a , very good reason for acting as they had done,hecause unless , the members of Parliament were compelled to act in the matter they would do as little as they possibly could. (Applause.) Mr. George Warburton impressively recited " The Pire- man's Wedding." Mr. Benjamin Harrison moved—" That this meeting is of opinion that the compulsory vaccination laws are cruel, unjust, and mischievous, inasmuch as they are the cause of very much injury to intents in the shape of blood poisonine, erysipelas, syphilis, scrofula, dm., without any correspond- ing equivalent in the form of protection from smallpox, which they erroneously assume ; experience teaching us that vaccination does not give the protection it pretends to offer. We would, therefore, call upon our legislators to re- peal the compulsory clauses of the Vaccination Acts t the earliest possible moment" He explained that the opera- tion of vaccination was performed upon intents when they needed all the vitality they could possibly have to battle with infantile diseases they had to pass through. All parents knew how many struggles children had to pass through, and he thought it was very wrong that they should be compelled to go under an operation which caused them excruciating pain when they were passing through infantile diseases. Not only was it cruel, but the law was unjust in asrnuch as the wealthy could evade it by paving the fines impased open them. Vaccination did not protect them from smallpox, for in hospitals a very large number of per- sons died after vaccination, and that was proof positive that it did not protect them. (Applause.) Mr. J. Pearson, in seconding the resolution, said the anti- vaccinators intended to work and fight until they got the compulsory clauses of the Vaccination Acts repealed. When the proper time came, at the ballot box, they must only vote for the candidates who would go in for the re- peal of the compulsory clauses of the Vaccination Acts. (Applause.) Dr. Robinson, of Dukinfield, on rising to support the mo- tion was warmly received. In the course of an impressive address he explained that 14 years ago the direction of legislation in regard to vaccination was towards compulsion,- but now, instead of making the laws more stringent, the legislators were speaking about diminishing the compulsion. As a sailor on the sea, he began to see land, and he thought the time was not far distant when the laws would be abso- lutely repealed. As a member of the medical profession, he said if there was anything in a medical idea it must not be put in an Act of Parliament. The idea of vaccination was the only medical remedy put into an Act of Parliament, for other medical remedies had to make their way into the world on their own merits, and subject to the criticism of every medical man. While the idea of inoculation or pro- tection from, disease had been enshrined in an Act of Par- liament, the idea itself had been continually changed, and there was nothing of the original left, except the fact of its compulsion and vested interest, and it had not driven small- pox out of the country. Alluding to statistics on vaocina- tion, he said that doctors only operated on strong and healthy children, so that the naturally unhealthy and weak remained on the one hand, and the strong on the other. The stWetics as to deaths in each class were therefore unreliable, and were no foundation for the claim that vaccination had protected the country. Smallpox was only one of several foreign diseasee, fncluding the black death, plague, ite., that , remained in this country, and it was the only one for which inoculation was said to be a remedy. In the case of the black death and plague they did not inoculate, and they were gone, but in the case of smallpox they did inoculate and the disease remained. (Applause.) He therefore came to the conclusion that if it had not been for inoculation smallpox would have been as much absent from the country its the Week death and the plague were. That was a startling fact, but history showed that it was so. Smallpox inoculation was the greatest curse that ever came upon the country ; bet there was a great deal of an- neceeeary alarm in the minds of thi3 people regarding small- pox. In its early stages there was no disease so amenable to commonsense treatment. It was for the people to say if they would soy longer submit to the gross tyranny, and he urged upou them that any man who would sit quietly under the despoti.ma was unworthy of being the head of an Eng- lish household. (Cheers.) When he knew that they had pure water, pure air, and good food, and that mon were being fined and imprisoned because they would not believe that diseaee protected health, he asked where was their boasted civilisation ? (Applause.) Mr. Jacob Bright had recently said at Manchester: "You talk about confiscation of property, but what is that to crushing the human mind ?" (Applause.) Mr. J, Williams then gave a ventriloquial entertainment, for which he was warmly applauded. Dr. G. Brown, president of the Society of United Medical Herbalists of Great Britain, gave a lengthy address on the evils of vaccination. He said that one of his children had been ill from its effects, and he denied that it was the slightest prot-ction against smallpox, any more than lifting an umbrella was a protection in a thunderstorm It was one of the greatest evils connected with the rising genera- tion, and he strongly urged young married people to thor- oughly consider the question before sending their children to be vaccinated. He maintained that probably one million pounds accrued to the medical profession each year through the practice of viccination, and he asked how under the circumstances they could expect the doctors to sty that it was not beneficial? (Applause.) But the time would come when the law would be repealed, and it was only for the people to make up their minds when it should be done, and then to give effect to their opinions by voting only for those parliamentary candidates who would go in for a repeal of the compute-Ay clauses of the Act. (Applause.) The Chairman urged upon the people to demand the re- peal of the Acts, and be prepared to vote for only those can- didates who would support them. After Mr. George Warburton had recited "The Cavendish Cross," the proceedings concluded with a vote of thanks to the speakers, on the motion of Mr. W. Gilmour, and seconded by Mr. A. Woffinden.

(Applause.) The object of those lectures was, of course, to stimulate public feeling, and to impart such instruction as might prove helpful to the working-men and the people generally. Mr. Bellingham, after rapidly touch- ing on the changes that had taken place in the country during the past fifty years by the march of progress, pro- ceeded to show that nature was truth. Truth and nature would bear the strictest investigation. Nature itsetf was greater than science ; the stars were greater than astonomy the rocks than geology, and plants than botany. In an in- teresting manner be pointed out lessons to be learnt from nature, remarking that every thing in nature seemed to be made to minister to man.—Votes of thanks closed the pro- ceedings.
PR ESCOT.
CARR'S COLLIERY.—The men received their strike pay on Wednesday as usual. Eleven day wagemen came out on strike this week also.

UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—Two sermons were preached on Sunday last by the Rev. J. W. Chisholm, of Liverpool, at the church in Victoria-place, Prescot. There were good con- gregations, and the collection, including the children's, amounted to £ll Hs.

PRESCOT CONGREGATIONAL CILORCR.-011 Sunday even- ing the Rev. James Johnston, pastor, took for his theme, "The good Earl of Shaftesbury," taking for his text, "A citizen of no mean city," Acts xxi., 39. He referred to his extraordinary labours and achievements on behalf of the Ten Hours' Bill, Mines Act, ragged schools, dec., as the -glory of this nineteenth century. C.E.T S., PRESCOT BRANCII.—The second meeting of the season in connection with this branch was held at the Houghton-street Schools, and was again of a very success- ful character,there being no standing-room to be had. The vicar, the Rev. H. A. Macnaighten occupied the chair. An admirable address was given by Mr. J. Cross Eccles (of St. Helens), principally on the Society far the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (of which he is a prominent member.) A vocal and instrumental entertainment followed.

PEACE SOCIETY.—The new Assembly Hall, Kemble- street, was well filled on Wednesday evening in response to an invitation to bear a deputation from the Liverpool Peace Society. The chair was taken at eight o'clock by W. W. Pilkington. JP., who was accompanied on the platform by Mr. Thomas Crosfield, the Rev. Herbert V. Mills, Mr. Thos. Snape, Mr. W. P. Thompson, and Mr. J. T. Marsh (bon. secretary). The Rev. Mr. Mills aid Mc. Thompson were the speakers. The resolutions were carried unanimously and with enthusiasm. Vote of thanks to the chairman closed.

BOARD OF GITARDIANS.—The fortnightly meeting woe held on Thursday at the Whiston Workhouse. The chair- man (Mr. Leatherbarrow) stated that in accordance with the recommendation of the committee, Me.srs. Jackson, Fisher, Newsome and'himself had visited Kirkdale schools and Fan- I tasaph Orphanage, where Preseot Union children were placed. At Kirkdale they were very pleased to notice the marked improvement in the children since their last visit ; and as regarded Pantasaph he (the chairman) wag never more satisfied with a visit to any place since his connection with the Board. The cleanliness and discipline there were really a credit to any public institution.—The Rev. Thomas Chambers said it rejoiced him to heat such a re- port, and he was quite sure the ratepayers would be glad also.—The Workhouse Master reported that there were 420 inmates this week, against 421 last week and 432 in the corresponding week of last year.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board approving of the proposal to in- crease the salary of Mr. Hale, workhouse master, ' to £l3O per annum, and that of Mrs Hale to £7O per annum.

ST. HELENS. MAYoIILL BENEFICHNCE. The Mayor (Alderman T. Cook) will give a banquet to the members of the Town Council, and gentlemen of the borough, at the Town Will, on the 29th inst and the annual dinner to the aged poor, provided by his Worship, will take place on the following day.

On Wednesday evening the Rev. J. P. Bellingham. of Sheffield, gave a lecture in the Viaduct Institute, Earlen- tos/li, to a large andience, his subject being " Lessons of Nature." The chair was occupied by the Rev. F. N. Shim. mm, who, prior to introducing the lecturer, remarked that personally he felt deeply interested in the work of that institute, and hailed with very great pleasure anything that tended to educate thoroughly the working-men belonging to that town. , They could not overlook that in the near future the affairs of the nation would be more fully en- trusted to the working classes than hitherto, and there was a etrong tendency at head-quarters t) place more power in the bands of thoroughly practical men. If, therefore, that institute sought to unite technical knowledge with a thoroughly practical acquaintance with the workings of trade generally, was it not in touch with the spirit of the times, and could they afford to overlook the fact that the work that was being done in the room underneath them that night would balm a direct bearing on the future ? Doubtlese, from among the young men who had received technical, and practical information in connection with that institute many would go forth to occupy-positions of honour and of very great trust. (Hear, hear.) WIT AND HUMOUR. Very rash—A boy with measles. Buckskin is proverbially deer. The lover sows his wild dotes. Scene from reel life—A. waltz. One who takes lots of interest in his business—The pawn- broker. DlET.—Doctor: "For dinner tqlre forty minutes."—Timid patient : "Would it be dangerous to add a piece of meat and some vegetables?" NO ROOK FOR DEBETE.—Pretty woman was made to put astonishing garments on, while ugly man was destined merely to pay for them. There is no nse in mincing words on a subjeot like that. Judge: "Do you understand what you are to swear to? " —Witness : "Yes, sah. I'm to swar to tell de truf."— Judge : "And what will happen if you do not tell it ?" Witness: "I 'spects our side'll win de case, sah." " I never could see any sense in Sherman's despatch to Corse to' hold the fort,'" said old Wamsutta who was not in the war, as he lay down his paper. "Row could the soldiers hold the fort? I always supposed a fort was made! to hold the soldiers," and the old man mused about it all the rest of the morning. OF COURSE.—" Can I see the Mayor?' inquired a mem- I ber of the City Council of the former's servant. " Not at present; he's at dinner." "But my business is very i important." "I cannot help it, sir ; his honour is at steak." _ . .

THE BOY'S ADVICE.—" Say," said the editor's little son, as he entered a store, "do you keep knives r "Oh, yes," responded the storekeeper, "we've kept them for years." "Well," returned the boy, starting for the door, "you ought to advertise, and then you wouldn't keep them so long." TEMPORARY SUSPENSION OF NATURAL LAW.—A Boston writer thinks that the sexes are drifting apart. We hold that this depends on circumstances. When mother suddenly brings a light into the dark parlour the sexes drift apart very suddenly, but there seems to be an affinity, as it were, when the light is turned down low or extinguished, which drifts the sexes together again. THEY VVIA.— FRI How THEY LOVED EACH

..EY WERE lENDS, AND - OTHER !--Soene—A public dinner. Brown is seated next to Smith, whose shirt-front is detorated with three magnificent diamond (?) studs. Brown: Excuse me, Smith, but I really can't help admiring those studs of yours.—Smith: Yes; I think they are pretty good.—Brown: Don't you think you run a great risk with them? I suppose you have them insured ?—Smith: Insured? No, I should be glad to do so; but there Isn't a company in existence that will take a risk of that sort.—Brown: 111:v dear fellow, I beg your pardon—there are several plate-glass insurance-offices in Glasgow ! --Bailie. BET TE THE SCIENTIET.—I have been reading in

a learned work on winged things that a family of hornets is composed of males females, and neuters and that the males just sit around and give orders, while the females and neuters do all the work about the house and gather in the daily provisions. The same high authority intimates that the male hornet does not sting, but is purely ornamental, as it were, courting ease each shining hour, stroking his blonde moustache, and wearing a glad smile all day long. I wish I could believe this of the male hornet; but I cannot. My confidence in him is weak, and no male hornet shall ap- proach very near to me, if I know it, until he has furnished satisfactory evidence that he does not carry a deadly weapon concealed .bout his person. I can recall the time when a family of hornets forced themselves inta my society without waiting for an introduction, and I don't want it to occur again. The details of the affair are quite indelibly fixed in my memory's archives. I shall never forget it, until memory's page is obliterated, and the congregation has passed around my defunct remains, and rendered an honest decision as to how I look in complete repose. A self-made man, having amassed a large fortune in busi- ness, was afraid that his descendants would become ashamed of their lowly origin. Ile therefore built a handsome house and bought a large relate, which he left to his eldest son, with the proviso that it was to be his so long as he kept a portrait of the founder of the house dressed as a workman and with a bag of tools in his hand over the dining-room mantelpieoe. If this portrait was removed, the estate was to pass away to strangers. As might have been expected, the portrait became more and more alt object of detestation to the nouveaux riches, and they would gladly have got rid of it if they could have done so without imperilling the family fortune. At last they hit upon the following expe- dient. They had a Crusader painted on the back of the old gentleman's portrait, and then hung the picture in the place assigned to it, turning the old gentleman with his face to the wall. Then, when inquiries were made as to the iden- tity of the man in armour, they said that this was a "portrait of the founder of the house," and they consoled themselves with the thought that, if this was not the exact truth, it was within three-quarters of an inch of it. PnEcontors Pays.—" Why don't you turn over a new leaf ?" "I will, pa, in the spring. Can't do it this time of year, you know."—" Your father is entirely bald, isn't he?" said a man to a eon of a millionaire. " Yes," replied the youth sadly, "I'm the only heir he has left."—Minnie (In- quisitive child): "Mamma, you told me that ladies should I always be first, didn't you ?'' Mamma: "Yes, my darling, certainly." Minnie: "Then, if you please, why wasn't I born before Willie ?"—A three-year-old little girl wan taught to close her evening prayer, during the temporary absence of her father, with "and please watch over my papa." It sounded very sweet, but the mother's amusement may be imagined When she added, "and you had better keep an eye on mamma too !"—lt was one of the good little boys from a Sundae school near Boston who gave this interpretation to a verse taught by his teacher : "Behold, a greater than Solomon is here !" " Hold a grater .to Solomon's ear !"—When at a loss to give the answer f" Cain " to a question relative to that individual, the teacher, to jog his memory, asked, "What does a man walk with ?" Quick as a flash came the reply, "A woman."— A little Brooklyn girl who had been sick for some time was just finishing her evening prayer with "Bless papa and mamma, and—and"—when she paused and looked up at her mother. "Well, my darling, what else?" " And please, Dod, oh, please let the debbil take all the nasty medicine home with him. Amen."— As he heard the door-bell ring, Mr. Jinks looked up and said: "Jimmie, answer the door." "I can't do it, pa." " Jimmie !!! " Well, pa, I'll answer it all right when it speaks to me first; but I can't do it before, can I?" And then Jimmie and the book Mr. links was reading ran a race to nee which would get out of the room first." MEDICINES ELASTIC STOCKINGS. CHEMICALS, DRUGS, &0., by parcels post, under 1,b., 3,1. —- - . Ilurrox TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION.—On Tuesday even- ing the usual weekly meeting was well attended, the room being quite full. Mr. W. D. Stoba, secretary, presided, and gave an address on the hindrance of drink in commercial life, which was followed by an evening's musical entertain- ment, contributed by members and friends of the associa- tion. Song, " All for the sake of Sarah," Mr. Saunders ; reading," The Genva guide," the chairman ; song, "The deep blue sea," Mr. H. Capper ; recitation, " The story of Old John," Master S. Lunt ; song, "I am waiting." Mr. P. Capper; reading, " That little vulgar boy," Mas- ter T. Whittaker; piano duet, "Cynthia,' Mr. and Miss Saunders ; reading, " The Pedagogue," Mr. P. Capper ; song," Tell her I love her," Mr. H. Capper; Lancashire sketch, "Ab o'th Yate's speech," Mr. Stubs. At the close, in response to the chairman's invitation, three persona signed the pledge, and were enrolled. CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY, HUYTON BRANCIL—The above held their first public gathering of the season on Monday at the Huyton and Roby Schools. The proceedings began wit* sumptuous tea, provided by Mrs. Griffiths, to which over 80 sat down. The tables were served by the following ladies :—Mesdames Fletcher and Evans, Miss Veever, the Misses Blezard, the Misses Field- , wick, eke., with the assistaNce of Messrs. E. B. Williams, J. J. Dawson, H. Rigby, H. Brown, J. Johnson, and J. Taylor. The Rev. J. W. Tyrer was present and conducted the sub- sequent proceedings, which consisted of an entertaining programme by a company of ladies and gentlemen from St. Helens. who came by the invitation of Mr. Fletcher ' • and an address by Mr. R Comyn, of Liverpool. The Iluyton &Bringers opened the entertainment by a performance on the handbells, for which they were re-called. Mrs. Evans gave a piano sole, and Mr. Sanders sang "A grave digger;' Miss A. Myers recited " The curse of drink ;" and Mr. Merrill created much laughter by his song, " All in his Sunday clothes ;" a recitation by Mr. J. Myers " A tem- perance appeal," was encored, and he gave a Lancashire sketch, " Owd Bowles' ghost ;" Mr. Sanders sang " Every bullet has its billet ." and Mr. 'Myers recited " British in- terests ;" Mr. Merrill was encored for his song "The muddle puddle porter," and sang" Avery careful man; Mrs. Myers by rEquest gave "On to victory." At the close of the meet- ing five new members joined the society. THANKSGIVING SERVICES AT THE HUYTON QUARRY WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—On Sunday three services were held in this place of worship to celebrate the harvest festival. The edifice was tastefully decorated with frnit, grain,'vege- tables, flowers, and foliage. The pulpit, which occupies the centre of the chancel, was completely bidden by a col- lection of the finest specimens. On either side surmounting the whole were corn and haystacks, the arch overhead being traced with evergreens. The transepts presented the ap- pearance of hanging gardens, beneath the texts wrought on a white ground with evergreen letters and border, "Jesus Said, I am the bread of life," and " Man shall not live by bread alone." In the left transept there was also a fine display, principally of vegetables. A text formed of ears of wheat, Thou crowuest the year with Thy goodness " occu- pied the gable of the edifice by the porch, and underneath a rote of miniature sheaves, which was also ornamented with garlands of foliage and oats; brackets containing choice plants, dm., were placed at intervals on the walls and win- dow sills. The decorations were carried out in a very tasteful manner by the following ladies and gentlemen : Misses Booth, Collins, Morris, Mrs. Waters, Messrs. R. and D. Kilshaw, Hewitson, Preston, Ctrinishaw, and Jones. The fruit, &c., were contributed by Messrs., W. L. McClure, Morice, Kilahaw, Wilkinson, and many other friends. The sermons, morning and evening, were preached by Mr. J. Bosomwortb, of Way.srtree, and the children's service in the afternoon was conducted by Mr. B. Preston. Addresses were given by Messrs. Bos.omworth, Grimshaw, and Jones ; the hymn, "Sowing the seed," was very effectively ren- dered as a solo by Miss Bertha Jones. Collections were ' made On behalf of the home mission. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER

' LONDON, Tatatants.t. Affairs do not grow any better in Eastern Europe. The best that can be said is that as yet war has been I avoided. But there is preparation for war on every harid. The powder magazine is filled and the lid uplifted. Any moment an explosion may occur, and when it comes it will be of a magnitude that will shake Europe. Owing chiefly to B,ussia, there is a lack of accord in the counsels of the Great Powers. At first suspected ef hexing fomented the revolution, Russia now stands almost alone in the endeavour to undithe work which the Roumeliots accomplished *hen they drove the Turkish Gover- nor across the frontier. The other Powers, includ- ing England—which through Lord Beaconsfield and Lord Salisbury is at the bottom of the whole business—admit the impossibility Of re-patching up the unnatural arrangement established by the Ber- lin Treaty. These conflicting opinions might with- out difficulty be unified. The chief danger lies in the impetuosity of the Servians, who have armed themselves to the teeth and are determined to go to war with somebody. A closer interest in Foreign affairs has been elici- ted in connection with Burmah, where the noto- rie us RingTheebaw has broken out in a fresh place. Having murdered most of his relations, including his mother-in-law, this maniacal mGnarch has cast his eyes upon the property of an Anglo-Indian com- pany and proposes to make it his own. Me has in- solently rebuffed a proposal for arbitration made by Lord Dufferin and seems determined to go his own way. H will, however, find that his new enter- prise is very different from the familiar one of slaughtering his uncles, his cousins, and his aunts. The civilised world has long hankered for an oppor- tunity of dealing with this lunatic, and he now seems to have provided it. Rumours of recent ad- vances of France towards obtaining a footing in Burmah are not calculated to stay the hand of Lord Dufferin in dealing firmly and finally with King Theebaw. The 17th of November is now authoritatively fixed for the dissolution, and as I have frequently stated in contradiction to varying rumours, the General Election will be over within the first week in December. In the meantime the campaign is being merrily carried forward. Mr. Chamberlain, not content with the sustained burst of oratory that closed a fortnight ago has taken the field again. On a single night we have speeches from Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Goschen, Sir HeF7 James, and Colonel Stanley, who must be chagrined at noticing what small measure of space the London news- papers spare him from the columns assigned to the Liberal orators. But in truth, except when Lord Salisbury or Lord Randolph. Churchill speak, dis- tressingly little attention is paid to utterances from the Tory side. From this time forward the strug- gle will increase in intensity. Mr. Gladstone is 'saving himself up" for his journey to Midlothian, which he wisely defers till somewhere near the eve of the election. He is reported to be in excellent health and spirits, anj. much cheered by the re- ports which reach him-from all quarters of the cer- tainty of a great Liberal triumph in the forthcom- ing contest. One thing is quite certain upon the least sanguine estimate. The opportunities for mischief of the present Government are strictly limited by time. They will next month be turned out of office by the popular voice. There remains the question new in English politics, whether the Liberals will have a majority large enough to counteract the alliance of Conservatives and Land Leaguers. I put this question the other day to a gentleman whose official position in the Liberal party makes him an authority. His answer was that Mr. Gladstone will have a majority of thirty- five over the combined forces of Mr. Parnell and Lord Salisbury. Mr. Labouchere, who has been consulted on the subject of the letter from Sir Henry Ponsonby with reference to the Queen's savings, replies very guar- dedly. In private conversation he is more frank. "If the Queen does not possess a million," I have heard him say, " she must have been very badly ad- vised in her investments." But it will be seen that Sir Henry Ponsonby's letter does not go so far as Mr. Labouchere here puts it. The occasion for the letter was a statement publicly made that the Queen had invested a million sterling in ground rents in London. Sir H. Ponsonby wrote that her Majesty did not possess a million to invest in ground rents or anything else. That is quite true, as it would be of a man who, having invested all his spare cash, declared that he had not a hundred to put in anything. Whether the Queen pounds saved a million sterling or, as I recently saw stated in America, possesses a fortune of eight mil- lions, is no business of ours, except in view of the fact that a certain annual sUm is provided out of taxation for maintaining the state of Royalty, and that sum is not expended in the manner originally -contemplated. This is a question that is settled by evidence of the simple senses. It is plainly impose sib's that a lady living in strictest seclusion, as it pleases the Queen to do, should be able to spend an annual income provided for a sovereign of a great empire. If the difference between the two classes of expenditure be not saved, it is either lost or stolen. Amongst the gossip which Sir Henry Pon- sonby's letter has given rise to is the statement that since the death of the Duke of Albany the Queen has made a new will. The Isle of Wight property. it is said, goes to the Duke of Connaught, Balmoral and the Scotch property to Princess Bea- trice. whilst handsome provision is made for the child of the Duchess of Albany. In the second portion of the Greville memoirs, issued to the public to-day, there is an interesting entry with respect to Macaulay. Greville asked a friend of the historian's by what process he had contrived to accumulate such boundless stores of information. The reply was that the secret rested in Macaulay's power of giving his undivided atten- tion to the book or the subject upon which he was occupied. Moreover, that as other men read by syllables, or by words, he had the faculty of reading by whole sentences, of swallowing as it were whole paragraphs at once. This is a gift which Lord. Macaulay enjoyed in company with Mr. Gladstone. I have often been surprised at the marvellous rapidity with which Mr. Gladstone masters a book. I have seen him sitting on the Treasury bench on a dull night with a Blue-book in his hand, evidently steadily reading it through, but turning over the pages with a rapidity that seemed to indicate he was merely skimming its contents. And yet, as appeared from subsequent speech, he had absolutely mastered its contents. It is the same with other classes of literature. He does not read novels as some of his colleagues in the late Cabinet do—Mr. Chainberlain, for example, while President of the Local Government Board, was never without a French novel in his dusky private room. But there are no important books coming forth which Mr. Gladstone has not read, and of which at his Thurs- day morning breakfasts he has not something to say. Arrangements have been definitely made by which our Royal family will become connected with the Orleans family. Prince Waldemar, of Denmark, is engaged to marry the Princess Amelie, eldest daughter of the Due de Chartres. Prince Waldemar is the youngest son of the King of Denmark, brother of the Princess of Wales. For the Orleans family, who have long been out in the cold, this is an ad- vantageous alliance. Not only does the daughter of the Due de Chartres become sister-in-law to the future kings of England and Denmark, but she Oc- cupies the same position towards the Czar and the King of Greece. This family of the King of Den- mark is one of the best married in Europe, and if Royal marriage alliances really meant anything, which in times of storm and stress they do not, he should be a powerful monarch. Oddly enough the Princess of Wales married into her own family when she became the wife of the Prince of Wales. Both her father . and mother are able to trace their direct descent from George the Second. A friend of mine whoThas been staying at Dinard tells me he frequently saw the young couple. The Prince is a light-haired youth of about twenty-six years. The Princess is *hie-eyed blonde of pretty, simple manners. Dinard is quite a home 'of ref uke for the Orleans Princes. They have spent the whole of the last summer there; the Due de Chartres, the Prince de Joinville, and the head of the household, the Comte de Paris. This Dinard has, like many watering places, a history. Twenty years ago it was a fishing village. Its natural beauties attracted the attention of an enterprising American, who bought the tongue of land upon which the village stood, and by way of commencement built a fine house for himself. He did not live to enter it, or to enloy, the fruits of his foresight. :But his widow still lives, and draws an immense fortune from the place, just as the Duke of Devonshire does from Eastbourne. The Prince of Wales once visited Dinard, a circumstance sufficient to make it attrac- tive to English society, which has of late years shown an increasing partiality to the little place. Among. its other claims to fame is the fact that Nicolinz, one of the late husbands of Patti, lived here. His father, who was named Nicolai, kept a public-house at Dinard, and the future tenor used to do the marketing.

THE EARLESTOWN FOOTPATH QUESTION. Sir,—The footpath question has at length been before the magistrates, bat the question cannot be said to be satisfactorily settled. The public either have a right to use the road or they have not, and as the chief obstruction has been erected on land that has always been held to be com- mon land would it not be better for the Commissioners to I send a staff of men and remove the obstructi&n. If Mr. Legh thinks an injury has been done him he has a proper remedy, and if the land does belong to him it should be a , vary easy matter for him to produce legal proof of owner- ' ship, iI trust the Commissioners will not allow the matter to rest in the present unsatisfactory condition, but have the case taken to a superior Court, which, as custodians of the public rights, I think they are in honour bound to do, and as I believe they have a good case, I hope they will also have a good lawyer. Will Mr. Leg!), or his agent, kindly furnish through your columns the name of the person from whom the said : land was purchased, and the date of transfer, or if it was cot a purchase by what means and when he became owner. , This should be an easy matter, if he is the ewner.—yours ',truly,

div.head: RATEPAYER.
div.p: RATEPAYER.
LIBER&LISM IN RUNCORN.

Sir,—The newly enfranchised, electors of Runcorn are looking forward with the profounilest inte.est to the forth- coming meeting of Liberals in the Public Hall. Hitherto the interest and delight which they took in such meetings were, to a very large extent, marred by the fact that, though they were at liberty to applaud the sentiments ex- pressed by a Warren or a Latham, they were unable to fol- low it tap on the day of election with their votes, because they were not "capable citizens," in the opinion of those members of Pa'rliarnent who now, as Conservative candi- dates, are eating dirt and their own words at the same time, to gain their support at the polls. What is their action in relation to parnellism but a disgraceful truckling to treason In order to gain the help of a few beggarly Irish votes in English constituencies at the election ? There will be a rude awakening for these Tory Rip-van-Winkles. They will find to their dismay that these men whom they kept voteless were not brainless, and had the geod sense to see through their clumsy schemes, and 'relegate them to that obscure lumber room, where they will meet with congenial companions equally wooden and useless. There are few towns the size of Runcorn where the working-men take so great an interest in political matters, and the G.O.M. Junior (if such an Irishism is permissible) will meet with a recep- tion that will prove to him bow intense and intelligent that interest is. The trammels of office have not pressed se tightly upon Mr. Herbert Gladstone that he need feir launching out on those subjects which the timid among his father's tollewers would seek to keep out of the present election campaign. He will find his audience robust enough to stand strong doses of Radicalism ; and if he may lilt feel disposed to supply the ardent Radicals with the pabulum they expect, it is to be hoped that Mr. Summers or some one else will keep Mr. Brunner in countenance. We must have no slipping back into the old ruts of Whiggism. —Yours, &c., RUNCORN HAD. Runcorn, October 14th, 1885.

THE FAIR TRADE MOVEMENT.—AN EXPOSURE OF TORY TACTICS. Sir,—The most interesting speech delivered by Mr. .1. Bright is a contribution to the Protection controversy, which will be fully appreciated by working-men throughout the kingdom. Our Tory friends may term it "Ancient history." This is true only in the sense that Protection also is a relic of other dais, and the attempt to revive it justi- fies those who have experienced its bitter fruits, is coming forward and laying before the people a short sketch of com- parative history. It is of little use pointing ont to our Tory friends that they are not agreed amongst themselves as to what they I mean by the various terms used by the party. Only the other day a Tory ex minister, Mr. J. Lowther, called out as loudly as ever for a tax to be placed upon imported grain. Lord Iddeeleigh. speaking at Sherbrooke Park, denounced this as "sheer nonsense,' having previously ridiculed it as a "pious opinion." All prominent Tories light shy of the question, not caring to show a flag that carries with it such sad reflections of a bitter past. As there is no likelihood of the Conservative leaders making Protection, Reciprocity, or whatever they like to call it, a national question, it is left to the discretion of the party managers in the different elec• toral districts to make such use of it as the circumstances of the case permit. In Warrington the party seem to think the people suffi- ciently gullible to be acted upon. It is very likely they will find out their mistake, more especially when it is re- membered that on the Fair Trade question they are all at sixes and sevens. Some of your readers will no doubt re- member the Parliamentary Debating Society we had in this town. One of the subjects brought forward by, I think, my friend the Rev.E.C.B. Carleton was the question of fair trade. iThe most enthusiastic and convincing speech on the Ques- tion was delivered against it by a Tory, Mr. G. Woods. This gentleman, interested as he lain the wire trade, told his Tory friends that no help was to be expected from Protection, and he voted against them. In spite of the knowledge the Tories possess respecting divisions in their camp on this question, they have persisted in bringing it forward at one ce their meetings in Sankey-street, with the result that, as a party question, Warrington Conservatism will know it no more. But this does not preclude the irresponsible mem- bers of the party from making capital out of it wheiiever possible. A paper claiming to be in the confidence of the party has taken upon itself the task of giving to the people of -Warrington Fair Trade physic; and with abject adula- tion of Sir Gilbert Greenall, which' no doubt, he will know how to value, claims the votes of the people for that gentle- man on the ground that he will support, what? Not Lord Salisbury in appointing a Royal Commission to inquire into the present depressed state of trade. They already have this ; but that he will support a Conservative Government in depriving England of the benefits of being, what Sir Staf- ford Nerthcote termed, "the centre aad place of exchange." No doubt, Sir Gilbert will, when he addresses the electors Of Warrington, on the 21st lost, give them the benefit of his wide experience, and say bow far he is prepared to go in support of the doctrine so assiduously put forward by the paper in question. It fair argument were used, no one would have any right to complain. but intimidation of a kind differing very little from what is now being practiced at Crewe is resorted to. In last iturday's issue appears the following : I am very sorry to learn that notwithstanding the reduc:lons the wire drawers have already suffered, it is generally under- stood that the manufacturers have been placed In no better position, as foreign competition Las still con hued to lecrease and it is therefore not unlikely that a furthtr reduction of wages may soon be asked for. This will surely bring the blessings of Free Trade home to the minds of those who have to stiffer by It. Let the wire drawers think of ~he facts that their manufacture Is shut nut of other contraries by means of heavy duties. Hence the foreigoers can get a good remunerative price at home, and can afford to send their surplus stock here and nodersell us. as freight is cheap and we ~ffer them every facility, and, in addi- tion to that, they are fast underselling us in many of our colonies for the same reason. When I read the above I was astounded at the impudence and ignorance displayed by the writer. Was this Tory writer giving a gentle hint to employers of what he would like to see? Or was he merely using a little bunkum to frighten a few ignorant voters into supporting his great commercial friend at Walton? However this might be, I determined to knode its real value. The wire manufac- turers of Warrington are not so mimerons but what one may soon run them over. To commence with the least first. At Longford Wire Mills, which is managed by Tories, and supported by Sir Gilbert's money, no union men, or men who have served their time to the trade, are employed, and the manager is a pronounced Free Trader. No reduction, I thought, could possibly take place at this shop, inasmuch as they do net at the present time pay the list price. With Hay Bridge the case is somewhat different. The great apostle of Fair Trade has here his abiding place, and no doubt a blind reliance on the benefits to accrue from Protection has caused the management to live "hoping on, hoping ever," but at leak, I think, they have no thought of a reduction. We have two steel mil's in the town, both under Tory control. Our friend of the Tory paper may be in the secrets of these establishments. He may also have been told that hitherto a monopoly has sustained a business, and that the breaking down of this monopoly has caused consternation. If so, I wonder he was not convinced of the utter absurdity of depending upon Protection, because I think that at least these two mills have not as yet suffered from foreign com- petition. nor have I heard of the employers being supporters of the Fair Trade craze. It but remains to refer to the two largest iron wire manu- factories in the kingdom—Messrs. Rylands' Brothers (Li mi.. bad), and the White Cross Wire Company (Limited.) With the view of getting at the bottom of the matter, I addressed the following letter to my respected employer, Mr. J. Rylands
17 ,11nnehesfmr-lane.

1 Fir,—l hope you will forgive me if lam at all indiscreet in , writing VOl2 with reference to the paragraphs in the paper I I.forward you by this post. YOU WI I notice that a pos-ible re- ' duct ion in wages is referred to. I feel conent that this is another "Tory Dodge" intended to frighten our workmen into voting for Sir Gilbert and " Fair Trade." If I am right In my conclusions, I should feel deeply obliged hy a commu• nieation that I could lay before the men or send to the Press.
—You rs respectfully, - J. Bylands, Esq. I received the following in reply:—
11. WHITHAM.
October 14th, 1885,

Dear Whitham,—The paragraph in the "Observer." to which you called my attention, is the first intimation I have had that there is an intention of reducing wiredrawers' wages. It is true tbat we still stiffer from German competl-

BIBLE STUDY IN WIDNES BOARD SCHOOLS. Last evening, Mr. J. Brock, J.P., distributed the prizes to the pupil teachers of the Widnes Board School who had been successful in the examination in Biblical knowledge. The prizes were given by Mr. R. 11. Davies, a member of the Board, and those students who attain the "first-class " position have the privilege of choosing from the following valu- able books ;—" Farrar's Life of Christ," "The Land and the Book," and the revised Bible. After a few remarks by Mr. Danby (clerk to the Board) Mr. Brock delivered an address to the teachers. He ex- , pressed his pleasure at being present to distribute I the prizes which had been so liberally provided by Mr. Davies, and referring to the Bible said they had I within the backs of that book everything they re- quired to guide them through life, to strengthen I them to resist temptation, to enable them to over- come every trial and live a faithfill and pure life, and at last come off the conqueror.
