FOREST BAZAAR AT WARRINGTON. Some eighteen months ago it was determined by the Wes- leyans residing at and near Sankey Bridges, that a chapel of suitable dimensions was necessary to meet the require- ments of an increasing community. Accordingly, with characteristic vigour, the work was taken in band, and , speedily accomplished, the result being seen in the conifer- table place of worship that has been erected on a site near the Liverpool-road, and in a very central position for those attending it. It is some time since the building was opened, and it is now filled Sunday after Sunday with a congrega- tion of devout worshippers, who have worked hard and patiently to clear off the debt that was incurred. Mainly by the self-denying efforts of the working people, who form the principal oat of the congregation, that debt had been reduced until only about £3OO remain to be paid, and on Wednesday a Forest Bazaar was opened in Bold-street Wes- leyan Schoolroom, with the object of raising that sum. The promoters formed the idea of arranging the stalls amid a miniature forest of fir trees and shrubbery, thus introducing an element of novelty that had a happy effect. The stalls, also, instead of, as usual, being built round the room, were more centrally placed, one, of considerable dimensions, be- ing erected in the middle of the floor, radiating from which were other stalls placed in triangular shape. The refresh- ment stall occupied a good position on one side of the building, and at the far end, erected near the wall, was the agricultural produce stall, stocked with all kinds of good things. The ante-rooms at the sides were devoted to vari- ous amusements. In one a working steamer and other boats voyaged to and fro on the smooth waters of an im- provised ship canal, and were captained by Messrs. Monks, Swift, and Summertield. Another contained an art museum, and vet another served as the "old curiosity shop." It almost goes without saying that once the bazaar was fairly begun these additional attractions drew into the coffers coin of the realm which, in the aggregate, must amount to no in- considerable sum. In the evening an orchestra, of which Mr. C. H. Pigot was the conductor, played sweet music to the enjoyment alike of the buyer and the seller. At the opening ceremony, which took place early in the afternoon, there was a fair number of visitors present. The Mayor of St. Helens (Alderman T. Cook), had consented to declare the bazaar open, and he was supported, among others, by Mr. J. U. McMinnies, M.P. for Warrington, Mr. W. Cros- field, J.P., Liberal carididate for the borough, the Revs. Jno. Yonge, J. McTurk, G. E. Cutting, and J. H. Jones, Dr. Mackie, Mr. it Garnett, J.P., and Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P. A hymn having been sung, and prayer offered, The Key. J. McTuarK heartily congratulated the Sankey Bridges friends on their preparation for the bazaar. After giving details as to the origin of the bazaar, he said be was sure that they all wished them great success. (Hear, hear.) He was pleased to sae so many who had come to the opening ceremony, and to find that the Mayor of St. Elelens was with them. He had the privilege of calling upon that gentleman to open the bazaar, but, before doing so he thought they would be glad if Mr. Mcalinniee would address them. Mr. Mc MINSIBS, M.P.. who was received with applause, said he had been at so many baziars that he bad had an idea of asking some of the ladies who were presiding at the meals if they had anything like a new speech that anyone could make at a bazaar. (Laughter.) Bazaars had become so frequent that, really, he had forgotten everything that he should say. There was a story told of an actor who, after performing 72 nights in one particular play, broke down in his part, and on being reproached by the manager said " How can a fellow remember a thing for ever? " (Laughter.) Undoubtedly baztars were getting very fre- quent and numerous. At the same time he had not lost his faith in them. He believed that was the best way of raising money for charitable and religious purposes. He had bad that opinion for many years, and had not lost it yet. He might say that the fact was that he ought to have been that day at another bezear—(leughter)—at a place thirty miles from Warrington, and he rather thought , that he promised to be both there and at War- rington. But they knew, as the Irishman said, a man could not be in two Places at once, barring he was a bird—(laughter)--and so it was not possible for him to be at the bazaar at Preston and the bazaar at Warrington. In reference to the increasing number of these bazaars, he remarked that if they were found to be too numerous they would not be supported, and the number would decrease, but , so long as bazaars were found to be profitable and, as he bee lievei they were, the best means of raisingmoney for religious , and philanthropic purposes, bazaars would be held. It had been said Lhat they expected, hoped, and wished to raise £3OO. He had had a great deal to do with bazaars in his time, but ; be never had to do with a bazaar that did not raise more money than they expected. (Laughter.) In conclusion he had only to say that-he hoped that the ladies would be very persuasive, the gentlemen very generous, and that they would realise more than they expected at that bazaar. (Ap- plause.) Dr. M %ME, who wee next asked to speak, remarked that of late he had been very much in the North, where they had been holding bazaars, that had been extraordinarily successful. In three cases they had been held on behalf of a church that WAS practically doomed Ito death in the minds of its opponents, but the people would not believe it. He hoped that the money required would he raised, and that, were it not, they would let him- self and Mr. McMinnies know at the last. tApplauee ) Mr. W. CROSFIELD, J.P., who was applauded in respond- ing to a request to speak, said that he recognised that they were there that day far practical business, and therefore he should but have few words to say. He did not feel in the same difficulty as Dr. Mackie or Mr. lilcMinnies, for he woe bound to say that he seldom went to bazaars. He acted upon tie principle that it was very much better to let his wife attend them—(laughter)—than to go himself, but inas- much as she wee to be engaged in taking part :at a bazaar in Liverpool the following day, he thought it hardly fair to aek her to come to Warrington that day ; therefore he was there instead. (Applause.) The reason that he had been to so few bazaars was that as a very little boy he took a very strone. prejudice against them. He once went to a great b izear held in Liverpool, when he was a youngster, and hie father gave him a shilling to spend at the bazaar. He was exceedingly anxious to lay out that shilling. He was afraid that he had not an interust in the baziZr first and foremost in his heart, but he had a strong desire to lay out the shilling in the best way he could for himself. He was particularly taken with an announcement of a marvel- lous development that was to be seen in one of the private roams—a wonderful combination of science and art—which he would be allowed to inspect on spending sixpence. He did so, and found that he was expected to look into R. looking- glass and see his own face. (Laughter.) He went away from that bazaar thoroughly disgusted. ( Renewed laughter.) He remembered that at the time it made each an impression on his father, that he went and protested against little children being taken in. Unlike Mr. McMinniee' friend, the acter, they would think, he had a long memory, for he remembered it yet. (Laughter.) Bazaars at the present

It is possible there, may be a large increase in the demand for wire, in which case we may expect higher prices, and you will hear nothing about reduction ot wages. Yours truly,

I also made it my business to see Mr. Biminill, the man- ager of White Cross, a gentleman well qualified to give an opinion on Fair Trade. Nothing whatever was known respecting any reduction. More than this, I was assured that neither he nor Mr. Carson, the managing director, bad any sympathy with the Fair Trade movement. In fact, the latter gentleman, who I may say is a deservedly respected member of the Tory party, described the Fair Irade movement as one "decidedly suicidal." I think I ' hive unmasked what I must term a bit of Conservative chicanery, and I think it is plain to be seen that if any re, duction is contemplated it mast be by Tory manufacturers, and that a Tory newspaper tkinks it a duty I. urge the matter rm.—Yours, dm., .

day were very different to what they were in those times. There were not now such wonderful combinations to serve

as traps for the unwary, and take away their money against their will. The bazaars of to-day were very much better conducted, and on much sounder principles when they were conneeied with religious objects, than they were in those days. He had before him a paper, showing the amuse- ments that were to be found at that bazaar. To some ex-

tent to relieve the monotony of going Dom one stall to anotbor, people could retire into adjoining vestries and amuse ihemselves. They would have a musical entertain- ment every hour, and he must congratulate them that they had already accomplished that which was a great engineer- ing enterprise of the present day, which had not as yet been carried out in its entirety, they had on their own account established a ship canal. (Laughter.) If he was right in identifying the room where the skip canal was, they had succeeded in the last act of that great work. They bad got water into the canal, but they bad not entirely succeeded in keeping it there. They bad also gone very near the verge of politics, for there was on view for one penny the Belgian bear. (Laughter.) He was rather anxious to kring his remarks to a conclusion, and spend his penny to see that Belgian bear. He never saw a Belgian bear, but pre- sumed that he was related to his near neighbour, the Rus- sian bear. (Laughter.) The old curiosity shop they could see for threepence, and they had also an art exhibition. Ile , concluded by wishing Success to the undertaking. (Ap- plause.) , The Itev. J. McTtrnst then explained that the Mayor of ' Warrington (Alderman Harrison) and Dr. Smith were un- able.to be present. . _ _ _

Alderman COOK, in declaring the bazaar open, said that he had undertaken that duty at the request ef Mr. Sum- mersgill, because he was told that the people of Sankey Bridges were very deserving, and had worked most indefat- igably towards the erection of the chapel. He was pleased to be there and to see the efforts they were making to clear off the debt. They had before them an indication of the earnestness of the people of Sankey Bridges, who after sub- scribing generously themselves, asked the public of War- rington and the neighbourhood to help them in their final effort. They had therefore got together a large number of articles that would suit every class, rich or poor. His im- pression was that they would raise the required sum of £3OO, as he never yet knew of a bazaar being a failure ; it was generally the case that more money was raised than Was expected, and he hoped it would be so in that instance. (Hear, hear.) It rested with the public, who were asked to buy the goods and would get a fair exchange for their money. The cause was a good one, he commended it to their careful consideration, and hoped that they would liberally support the bazaar. (Applause.) On the motion of the Rev. G. E. CUTTING, seconded by Mr. R. GARNETT, and supported by Mr. SIIMMERSGILL, Alderman Cook and the other gentlemen who had given addresses were cordially thanked, after which the sale was briskly proceeded with. The following is a list of names of the etall-holders :—(1) Mesdames Summersgill, Highley, &eddy, and Atkinson, and the Misses Summersgill and Highley ; (2) Mesdames Hough, Graham, Warlow, Tonge, and Barlow; (3) Mes- dames George, Lawton, Catterall, Walker, and Braithwaite; (4) Mesdames Blythe, Wood-yard, Pritchard, Gilman, Carrodine, and Light ; (5), scholars' stall, Mrs. Pacey, and Messrs. Snoddy and George,•, (6), refreshment stall, Mesdames Cook, Summerfield, Williamson, Horton, and Miler; (7) agricultural produce stall, Messrs. Summersgill and Brough, and the Misses Bennett. The sale was continued with great success on Thursday and yesterday. Last evening the financial result was an- nounced to those present by Mr. Snoddy. In the aggregate over £2OO was drawn. Mr. Sammersgill stated that £55 had been promised towards the building fund. The total cost of the building, including £93 for land to be invested as a guarantee fund, amounted to £1343. With the money already raised, including that promised, they would only require £27 to clear off the debt. The actual cost of the building was paid off, also a sum towards the capitalising of .he ground.

CRUELTY TO A HORNE.—EIa Monday Jas. Marsh, farmer, Lymm, was charged at the Petty Sessions at Altrincham with ill-treating a horse at Lymm on the let of last month. —lnspector Greenwell, of the and P.C. Dutton spohe to seeing the horse, which was suffering from ring- bone, being worked whilst in great pain, and Mr. Harrison, veterinary surgeon, of Altrincham, said that the animal was unfit to be worked.—As defendant had since destroyed the horse, he was only fined 10s and costs. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—A paper on a Burn's Pilgrimage" was read by the president of this association (Mr. Dodds), at the weekly meeting of the society, on Mon- day night. Mr. Dodds gave an interesting description of his tour in Scotland, when he visited the house where Burns was born, where he was married, and the house in which he died, giving also a description of the country through which he passed. There was a good attendance of members, the appreciation of the address being testified by a hearty vote of thanks accorded to Mr. Dodds. EXTRAORDINARY CONDUCT OF LABOURERS.—At Altrin- chain Petty sessions, on Monday, two Lye= labourers, named Joseph Eaves and Wright Taylor, were brought up in custody on charges of being drunk and disorderly at Heatley on the 4th inst, assaulting P.C. Buchanan and do- ing damage to his uniform. Another labourer vitiated Burks, also of Lymm, was, it was stated, corning from his work on the afternoon ot the day in question' when he met the two prisoners, who were in company with othtr men. On his approaching them Eaves said " Here's an Irishman ; let's- upset him." He then began kicking Burks, who was as- saulted by the other men also, thrown over a hedge into a pig-cote, and then on to a manure heap. Inforreation was given by a woman, who had seen the occurrence, to P.C. Buchanan, who went and demanded the names of the pri- soners. They, however, refused to give the information, and Eaves beat the policeman in the face unmercifully. They then got him down and otherwise assaulted him, until assistance came. Evidence bearing out this statement hav- ing been called, the prisoners were each sent to prison for a month with hard labour.

MR. LEADAM AT BROOM EDGE. Mr. T. 8. Leadam. the Liberal candidate for the Altrinc- barn Division, addressed a meeting on Monday evening at the Jolly Thrasher Inn, Broom Edge, near Lymm. There was a good attendance. The chair VI,S occupie4 by Mr. J. A. Swanwick, who was supported by Messrs. B. McKay, W. Ashcroft, and Cameron. Mr. LEADAM alluded at the outset to his speeches de- livered recently in the neighbourhood of Jytom, and also stated that he had referred to the career of the two great political parties from 1783. to 1832. Fifty years of .the Liberal Government, he argued, had been marked by fresh statutes being enacted conducing to the welfare and freedom of the working classes, and if the Liberals were again re- turned to power there were prospects in the future of more beneficial legislation for them. Mr. Le idam then referred

to some remarks which hid been made by Mr. Brooks with regard to the "overcrowding, filthy, unhealthy, and un- happy homes of the working climes." For 40 years, he (Mr. Leadam) desired to save the Liberal Government had been passing measwes for senitary legislatien—(applauee) —and after those 40 years the Tory party was awakening up only to find that there was something to be done and claimed all tire credit for moving in the matter. Lord Salis- bury had expressed himself in favour of appointing a com- mission of impairer into the conditions of workmen's dwell- ings in large towns, but said nothing about those in the country. The reason why the Conservatives were opposed to a commission of inquiry into the country dwellings was because they had to work with the parson and the squire. They had, however, a Royal Commission nominated by Mr. Gladstone. with Sir Charles Dilke as the chairman. After dealing with the Cooservative opposition to the various measures of reform, and remarking that the Conservatives trek credit for passing measures which had been brought about by the Liberals, he continued, even Mr. Plimsoll's Shipping Bill appeared as A Conservative measure—(laugh- ter)--and they would next be told that the extension of the franchise was brought about by the Conservative party. (Laughter.) He said either Mr. Brooks intended to raise the price of wheat to 50e per quarter, or he did not. If Mr. Brooks proposed to raise the price of bread, he (M. Leadam) asked whether workiee-men would support him ? (Cries of " No.") If Mr. Brooks was not sincere in what he said, he asked whether the farmers would support Mr. Brooks. (Hear, hear.) What farmers required was a thorough evs,em of agricultural reform. What they wanted was com- pensation for those improvements which they had executed before the Agricultural Holdings Act of 1833. They wanted power to execute improvements on farms without the con- sent of the landlords. They required absolute freedom of cultivation. (Applause ) They wanted free sale of improve- ment, and they must have land courts established for fixing fair vent. (Hear, hear.) They must have the Agricultural Holdings Act of 1883 so modified and improved as to pre- vent .the inadrquate compensation which now obtained. They muet have a system for the protection of the existing tenant. If these changes were made the position of the farm labourer, as well as the tenant farmer, would be im- proved, as more labourers would be employed on the lend than at present. If power was to be given to the local authorities they must be constituted in a different manner to what they sow were. (Hear, hear, and a Voice : " Not of landlords or agents!) The Liberals had confidence in the future, but the Conservatives had distrust of any- thing that was likely to happen. The Liberals were anxious to see progress, and were also desirous of leaving the world a little better than they found it. (Applause.) Various questions were put end satisfactorily answered. —Mr. CAMERON then moved—" That this meetiug desires to express its confidence is Mr. Leadam as a fit and proper person to represent the Altrincham Division in Parliament. and pledges itself to use all legitimate means to secure his return."—Mr. McKay seconded the proposition —Mr. HALL than addressed the meeting at cousiderahle length, cud ex- pressed the hope that the tight would be fought ins friendly manner.—Mr. T. STELFOE said he had always voted Con- servative, but was now willing to give his support to the candidate who offered to do his utmost to benefit the farmera—The resolution was then put to the meetieg and carried.—A rote of thanks to the Chairman brought the proceedings to a close.

FOOT RACE AT WALTON ARCITES.—On Saturday afternoon a race was run off on the canal bank near Walton Arches between John Thomason and Chas. Jones, young men, both of whom are employed at Messrs. Crosfield's soap works, The distance was 80 yards, the 'stake being £2 a side. An even start was made, and after a good race Jones won by about a yard.

MILITARY lilovinmrrs.—On Saturday ttidetach- ment of the 2nd Dragoon Guards (Scots Greys), comprising four officers, 72 men, and 83 horses, who were en route from Edinburgh to Aldershot, arrived in Warrington, where they were billeted until Mon- day morning, when the match was resumed. On Tuesday a second detachment of Scots Greys, en route from Glasgow to Aldershot, arrived in Warrington, where they remained until Wednesday morning.

Mr. Arrowsmith and the late Hugh Conway have much to answer for The success of 4,' Called Back," published in shilling form, has brought into the market a motley crew, each with his shilling book, more or less bad, chiefly more. They are becoming a drug upon the bookstalls, .and will shortly work , out their own cure. There has been nothing like , ithe success of "Called Back," nor is there likely to I I be. I am told that not less than 330,000 copies I were sold. The sale of "Dark Days" has passed its 200,000. This is better than writing or publish- ing three volume novels at a nominal price of a :iguinea and a half.

Lord Ripon has appointed Mr. Samuel Rowlandson, tenant farmer, to the Yorkshire Magisterial Bench. Over 1000 cattle sent by rail from Cork were despatched to the Englieh market from Waterford on Friday. The Oldham strike is expected to terminate by the accept- ance of five per cent reduction now, and at the end of three months to reconsider the question. Two Bridlington fishermen, brothers, named Abraham and Ralph Sanderson, were drowned while off that port on Friday, by the capsisiog of a coble in a rough sea. A telegram has just been received at Dover from the Hotel do Rivoli, Paris, stating that Lord Strathnairn, Field Marshall, died there about half-past six on Friday morning. Mr. Harold Wright, barrister, has accepted an invitation to contest the Chorley division of North-Lancashire in the Liberal interest, against General Fielden, the Conservative candidate. At Walsall Station, on Friday morning, Mr. William Thomas, solicitor, was killed at the level crossing. De- ceased was Mayor some years ago, but had retired from public life. Over 1,000 men and a number of boys employed at the Stupley Collieries, near Ilkeston, struck work on Friday against a proposed increase in the price of coal allowed to married colliers. MEMORIAL TO LORD SHAFTESBURY.—A large and in- fluential meeting was held at the Mansion House, London, on Friday afternoon, under the presidency of the Lord Mayor, for the purpose of promoting a national memorial to the memory of the late Lord Shaftesbury. The Earl of Granville proposed the resolution in favour of the proposed memorial. THE EASTERN CRISIS. MARCH OF THE BULGARIAN ARMY ON ADRIANOPLE. Intelligence has been received in Athens stating that Prince Alexander at ties head of his army, has left Phillip- popolis, and is marching towards Adrianople. MOVEMENT OF SERVIAN TROOPS. VIENNA, FRIDAY ArrEincoow.—A Belgrade telegram published by the 2Vew hree Press states that Servian troops crossed the Bulgarian frontier last night. The news is not confirmed. The Prince of Wales has left for Paris. OPINION OF MR. GLADSTONE. Mr. Gladstone, writing to a Bulgarian deputy in London, says he entirely deprecat-s movements like those appar- ently threatened by Servia and Greece, whose title to in- trigue with countries beyond their own borders he is unable to recognise. SIXTEEN LIVES LOST. BOMBAY, FRIDAY.—One of the nooses in the Baziar fell in to-day. Sixteen persons were killed and eleven seri- ously injured. THE CHOLERA. ROME, FRIDAY. Up to midnight yesterday there were 54 cases of ctiolera and 23 deaths in the Province of Palermo. EARTHQUAKE AT PALE RMO.—MANY PERSONS KILLED. A telegram from Palermo states that a large house there was thrown down yesterday morning by earthquake shocks. A number of persons were buried in the debris. Eight bodies have already been recovered.
